nodes.title: Disclosures in relation to specific circumstances
nodes.heading: Disclosures in relation to specific circumstances (1.1.2)
nodes.start_phrase:
In the context of the double materiality assessment (see section 1.4.1), different time intervals as opposed to those defined in the 
ESRS were applied to determine the financial materiality of the risks, as these are also used in our ESG risk management and 
decision-making processes:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and basis: The Sustainability Statement is prepared on a consolidated basis aligned with the consolidated financial statements. Several consolidated subsidiaries are exempt from issuing their own sustainability statements: CBC Banque SA (BE), Československá Obchodní Banka a.s. (CZ), K&H Bank Zrt. (HU), United Bulgarian Bank AD (BG), KBC Insurance NV (BE), and ČSOB Pojišt’ovna a.s. (CZ).
- Value chain coverage: Beyond own operations, the Statement includes material impacts, risks and opportunities from the upstream and downstream value chain, informed by due diligence and a double materiality assessment.
- Transparency on omissions: KBC did not use exemptions to omit trade secrets or information on impending developments/negotiations.
- Time horizons for materiality: For financial materiality of risks, KBC applies 0–3 years (short term), 3–10 years (medium term), and >10 years (long term), diverging from ESRS; CSRD-prescribed horizons are used for opportunities.
- Measurement uncertainty: Several key metrics involve data availability/quality constraints and methodological assumptions:
  - Total GHG emissions measured at 30 Sep 2024 as a proxy for 31 Dec 2024, with plans to shift to 31 Dec.
  - Scope 1: Use of Gross instead of Net Calorific Value where NCV is unavailable (slight overestimation).
  - Scope 2: For some EVs, offsite charging estimated via distance (limited overestimation).
  - Scope 3 (lending): PCAF standard with data quality scores; proxies/sector averages used where needed.
  - Scope 3 (asset management, sovereign bonds, own insurance investments): External provider data with estimates when issuer data is absent.
  - Insurance-associated emissions: PCAF Part C (Belgium), using exact vehicle data or country proxies; commercial lines use PCAF emission factors.
  - Internal carbon price: Scenario-based measurements, inherently uncertain.
- Incorporation by reference: ESRS 2 GOV-1 and GOV-3 disclosures are referenced to the Corporate Governance Statement (including Remuneration Report). Broader ESG risk management is explained at a high level in the Statement, with details in the KBC Risk Report (not externally assured) on www.kbc.com.
- Governance and diversity (as at 31-12-2024): Overview of composition for ExCo, RCC, AC, NC, RC, and the Board, covering executive/non-executive and independent members, tenure, age, gender, nationality, and qualifications. Highlights include:
  - ExCo: 7 executives; 1 woman/6 men; average age 57; nationalities mainly Belgian with Czech and Bulgarian members.
  - Board: 16 members; 5 women/11 men; 13 non-executives (3 independent); average age 59; average tenure 9 years; predominantly Belgian nationality with Spanish and Czech members; qualifications largely in law and economics/finance.
  - No employee/worker representation on these bodies.
  - Confirmation that bodies collectively possess required skills and experience per the Corporate Governance Charter.

nodes.title: Role of the administrative, management and supervisory bodies
nodes.heading: Role of the administrative, management and supervisory bodies (1.2.1)
nodes.start_phrase: In the table below, we show the composition and diversity of the members in the administrative, management and supervisory bodies.
nodes.summary:
- Document scope and references: Section of KBC Group’s 2024 Annual Report detailing sustainability governance and ESRS disclosures. ESRS 2 GOV-1 and GOV-3 requirements are incorporated by reference to the Corporate Governance Statement (incl. Remuneration Report). ESG risk management is summarised in the Sustainability Statement; further detail is in the non‑assured KBC Risk Report at kbc.com.

- Governance structure and roles:
  - Board of Directors: sets sustainability strategy and risk appetite (incl. ESG), approves major policy changes, oversees implementation via a Sustainability Dashboard, and monitors top sustainability risks (with RCC). AC oversees sustainability reporting processes.
  - Executive Committee (ExCo): operational management and implementation of ESG strategy and policies, assessment of ESG impacts/risks/opportunities, internal controls, and pursuit of ESG-related opportunities within group strategy.
  - Key committees and forums:
    - Internal Sustainability Board (ISB): principal ESG forum; chaired by Group CEO, vice‑chaired by Group CFO; met nine times in 2024.
    - Sustainable Finance Steering Committee: oversees climate and environmental themes (biodiversity, water, circularity); reports to ExCo and Board.
    - CSRD Steering Committee: oversees CSRD programme.
    - Data & Metrics Steering Committee: manages sustainability data and reporting challenges.
  - Group Corporate Sustainability: develops and supervises strategy, prepares the Sustainability Dashboard; led by Senior GM reporting to the Group CEO.
  - Country Sustainability General Managers and local sustainability departments/committees: integrate strategy locally, communicate, and provide/validate non‑financial information.
  - External advisory: External Sustainability Board (ESB) advises on policy/strategy; RI Advisory Board oversees screening of responsible investment funds.

- Integration with risk management:
  - ExCo designates climate and environmental risk, cyber risk, compliance risk and conduct risk as top risks; RCC and Board closely monitor them.
  - ESG risks embedded in the Three Lines of Defence and Risk Management Framework.
  - Monitoring and reporting cadence:
    - Sustainability Dashboard to ISB, ExCo and Board twice a year; progress influences ExCo variable remuneration.
    - Climate Risk Dashboard reported semi‑annually to ExCo and Board as part of the Integrated Risk Report.
    - Integrated Risk Report presented to Board, ExCo and RCC eight times per year, regularly covering ESG topics.
    - Compliance reporting: quarterly to ExCo and RCC; annually to the Board.
    - HR reporting to ExCo on hiring, performance, engagement and training; annual Diversity & Inclusion report; selected HR topics (e.g., succession) annually to ExCo and Board.

- Composition and diversity highlights (as of 31‑12‑2024):
  - Executive Committee: 7 executive members; gender 1 woman/6 men; nationalities 5 Belgian, 1 Czech, 1 Bulgarian; average age 57; average tenure 6 years; qualifications (approx.): law 29%, economics/finance 29%, MBA 14%, actuarial/insurance 14%, other 14%.
  - Board of Directors: 16 members (3 executive, 13 non‑executive incl. 3 independent); gender 5 women/11 men; age distribution 41–50: 1, 51–60: 8, >60: 7; average age 59; average tenure 9 years; nationalities 14 Belgian, 1 Spanish, 1 Czech; qualifications (approx.): law 25%, economics/finance 31%, MBA 17%, actuarial/insurance 6%, other 19%.
  - Committees (gender/nationality snapshots): 
    - RCC: 3 women/2 men; 3 Belgian, 1 Spanish, 1 Czech.
    - AC: 2 women/1 man; 1 Belgian, 1 Spanish, 1 Czech.
    - NC: 2 women/3 men; 4 Belgian, 1 Czech.
    - RC: 1 woman/2 men; 2 Belgian, 1 Spanish.
  - No employee/worker representation in the listed bodies.
  - Conclusion: bodies collectively possess required skills and experience per the Corporate Governance Charter; details in the Corporate Governance Statement.

- Skills, suitability and training:
  - Collective suitability matrix for Board and ExCo explicitly covers sustainability, climate/environment risks, cybersecurity, business conduct, and ability to assess risk/audit/compliance outputs; members develop expertise as needed.
  - New Board members receive onboarding including a briefing by Group Corporate Sustainability; ongoing training for Board and ExCo; engagement with internal and external ESG experts.

nodes.title: Information provided to and sustainability matters addressed by the undertaking’s administrative, management and supervisory bodies
nodes.heading: Information provided to and sustainability matters addressed by the undertaking’s administrative, management and supervisory bodies (1.2.2)
nodes.start_phrase: As mentioned above, twice a year the KBC Sustainability Dashboard is presented to the ISB, ExCo and the Board.
nodes.summary:
- Governance competence on sustainability: KBC uses a collective suitability matrix for the Board and ExCo that explicitly covers sustainability, including climate and environmental risks, cybersecurity, business conduct (e.g., AML/CFT), and the ability to scrutinize risk, audit and compliance reporting and functions. New members receive sustainability onboarding with the Senior General Manager of Group Corporate Sustainability, ongoing training includes ESG topics, and leaders consult internal and external ESG experts as needed.

- Information flow and oversight: Twice yearly, the KBC Sustainability Dashboard is presented to the ISB, ExCo and Board; these bodies also regularly review the corporate sustainability strategy, Sustainable Finance Programme progress and external sustainability reports. HR reports regularly to the ExCo on workforce topics (headcount, hiring, performance, engagement, training) and annually on diversity and inclusion; selected HR topics (e.g., succession) are reported yearly to ExCo and Board.

- ESG risk integration: ESG risks are embedded in the Risk Management Framework. An Integrated Risk Report—often with ESG items and a Climate Risk Dashboard—is presented eight times a year to the Board, ExCo and RCC. The RCC advises the Board, while ExCo is supported by committees such as the Group Lending Committee and Asset/Liability Committee. Compliance matters are reported quarterly to ExCo and RCC and annually to the Board, including breaches and remediation.

- Material topics addressed by governance bodies in 2024: Climate change (mitigation, energy, adaptation), water and marine resources, biodiversity and ecosystems, own workforce (working conditions; equal treatment and opportunities; privacy), consumers and end-users (information and cybersecurity; social inclusion), and business conduct (ethics and corporate culture; supplier relationships). These link to the company’s double materiality impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs).

- Incentives tied to sustainability: At least 30% of the ExCo’s collective variable remuneration is linked to sustainability performance, reflecting the three pillars of KBC’s sustainability strategy. Climate-related components—primarily progress against GHG reduction targets, development of sustainable products, own ecological footprint and stakeholder satisfaction—account for roughly 8–10% of ExCo variable pay. Sustainability metrics also influence the overall assessment used to determine remuneration.

nodes.title: Statement on due diligence
nodes.heading: Statement on due diligence (1.2.4)
nodes.start_phrase: Throughout this document, we touch on various aspects of our due diligence process with regard to material sustainability matters.
nodes.summary:
- The excerpt outlines KBC Group’s due diligence approach for material sustainability matters and maps each core due diligence element to specific sections of its Sustainability Statement.
- Embedding due diligence: Governance, strategy, and business model integration are covered, including board oversight (section 1.2.2), incentive alignment with sustainability performance (1.2.3), and the linkage of material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) to strategy and business model (1.3.3).
- Stakeholder engagement: Engagement with affected stakeholders is described across general stakeholders, own workforce, and consumers/end-users (1.3.2), with governance touchpoints (1.2.2), processes for identifying and assessing material IROs (1.4.1), and topic-specific policies on climate, water, biodiversity, workforce, and consumers (sections 2.2.2.1, 2.3.1.1, 2.4.2.1, 3.1.1.1, 3.2.1.1).
- Identifying and assessing adverse impacts: Methods and processes are detailed in 1.4.1 and connected to strategic implications in 1.3.3.
- Taking action on adverse impacts: Concrete actions span climate (2.2.2.2), water (2.3.1.2), biodiversity (2.4.2.2), own workforce (3.1.1.4), and consumers/end-users (3.2.1.4).
- Tracking effectiveness and communicating: Targets and performance tracking are provided for climate (2.2.3), water (2.3.2), biodiversity (2.4.3), workforce (3.1.2), consumers (3.2.2), and business conduct (4.1.2), supported by metrics for climate (2.2.3.2–2.2.3.4), workforce (3.1.2), and business conduct (4.1.2).
- Risk management and internal controls over sustainability reporting: KBC describes a groupwide, hierarchically validated reporting process that has evolved with regulatory and voluntary frameworks.
- Reporting governance: The Finance department coordinates the Sustainability Statement to ensure ESRS compliance; data is consolidated at group level with robust internal controls, including the four-eyes principle.
- Data ownership and challenge: Each data point has a designated lead and identified contributors/challengers across core countries.
- Oversight for CSRD: A dedicated CSRD Steering Committee oversees and manages implementation of CSRD-related reporting processes.

nodes.title: Risk management and internal controls over sustainability reporting

structure.title: Strategy
structure.heading: Strategy (1.3)
structure.start_phrase:
KBC is an integrated bank-insurance group (banking, insurance and asset management), mainly active in Belgium, Bulgaria, the 
Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia (our core markets).
structure.summary:
- Governance of CSRD reporting: A CSRD Steering Committee with senior leaders from Sustainability, Finance, Risk, Credit Risk, HR and Compliance oversees the process. The Sustainability Statement Approval Committee approves the statement before ExCo, Audit Committee and Board review and approval.
- Sustainability reporting risks and mitigations: 
  - Regulatory risk: Continuous monitoring of changing rules and guidance.
  - Data quality/verification risk: Use of trusted ESG data partners; checks on input; sustainability data managed via KBC’s Data & Metrics project with its own Steering Committee across core countries and group functions.
  - Legal/compliance/reputational (greenwashing) risk: Reliance on factual information and internal controls, including the four-eyes principle.
  - Operational risk: Drive automation of sustainability reporting; Data & Metrics Steering Committee manages data collection and reporting challenges.
  - Ongoing enhancements and periodic committee updates; internal audits in 2024 on double materiality assessment and EU Taxonomy reporting.
- Strategy and business model: KBC is an integrated bank-insurance group (banking, insurance, asset management) focused on Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia, with limited presence elsewhere to support corporate clients. Provides a wide range of financial products via branches and online channels, targeting retail, private banking, SME and midcap clients, and supports client sustainability transitions.
- Strategic principles: Client centricity, a bank-insurance+ experience, sustainable profitable growth and assuming a role in society; further details in the “Our strategy” section (not externally assured).
- Workforce footprint (31-12-2024): Belgium 14,553; Czech Republic 11,432; Slovakia 3,279; Hungary 3,912; Bulgaria 6,338; Rest of world 415; Total 39,929.

nodes.title: Strategy, business model and value chain
nodes.heading: Strategy, business model and value chain (1.3.1)
nodes.start_phrase:
KBC is an integrated bank-insurance group (banking, insurance and asset management), mainly active in Belgium, Bulgaria, the 
Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia (our core markets).
nodes.summary:
- Governance and assurance for sustainability reporting under CSRD: oversight by a CSRD Steering Committee with senior leaders from Sustainability, Finance, Risk, Credit Risk, HR and Compliance; Sustainability Statement approved by the Sustainability Statement Approval Committee, then reviewed/approved by ExCo, Audit Committee, and Board; committees are periodically briefed.
- Key sustainability reporting risks and mitigations:
  - Regulatory: evolving rules/standards; mitigation via close monitoring of regulatory landscape and guidance.
  - Data quality/verification: lack of standardization in external ESG data; mitigations include using trusted ESG data partners, data checks, and KBC’s Data & Metrics project with its own Steering Committee covering all core countries and group functions.
  - Legal/compliance/reputational (greenwashing): mitigated through factual disclosures and internal controls, including the four‑eyes principle.
  - Operational: integration into systems/processes can cause inefficiencies/errors; mitigation through increased automation and governance by the Data & Metrics Steering Committee.
  - 2024 internal audits covered the double materiality assessment process and EU Taxonomy reporting.
- Strategy and scope: KBC is an integrated bank‑insurer (banking, insurance, asset management) active mainly in Belgium, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia, with limited presence elsewhere to serve corporate clients; focus on retail, private banking, SME, and midcap clients; supports clients’ sustainability transitions; strategic principles include client centricity, a bank‑insurance+ experience, sustainable profitable growth, and societal responsibility.
- Workforce: total headcount 39,929 (Belgium 14,553; Czech Republic 11,432; Slovakia 3,279; Hungary 3,912; Bulgaria 6,338; Rest of world 415).
- Sustainability strategy aligned to SDGs:
  - SDG 3: promote employee work‑life balance; products enhancing healthcare, quality of life, and road safety.
  - SDG 7: promote renewable energy and efficiency; phased out thermal coal; restrictions on oil and gas per Energy Policy.
  - SDG 8: support entrepreneurs, start‑ups/scale‑ups (with focus on female entrepreneurship); microfinance/microinsurance in the Global South for financial inclusion.
  - SDG 12: products for low‑carbon/circular business; Responsible Investing as first/preferred solution.
  - SDG 13: portfolio climate targets aligned with Paris Agreement; engagement with clients/investees; reduce own footprint.
  - Framed objectives: limit adverse impacts (SDG 7/12/13), increase positive impacts (SDG 3/7/8/12/13), and enhance financial resilience (SDG 8); strong emphasis on employee capability building.
- Business model: create sustainable value as a bank (lending, sustainable investments) and insurer (risk reduction), leveraging workforce, digital/physical distribution, stakeholder relations, and financial capital; impacts considered across the value chain.
- Value chain overview:
  - Upstream: ICT, services (including HR/professional services), facilities (e.g., electricity, office furniture).
  - Own operations: HR, infrastructure, sales/marketing and partnerships, product development and data handling, business conduct and supplier relations.
  - Downstream: lending; asset management/investments; (re)insurance; other financial services (factoring, leasing, fleet management); non‑financial services (real estate, roadside assistance, employee benefits, start‑up support); includes community considerations.
- Stakeholder engagement: affected stakeholders (clients, employees, suppliers, society at large, with nature as a silent stakeholder) and users/readers of the Sustainability Statement (investors, core shareholders, public authorities, business partners, trade unions, NGOs, governments, academics, analysts); ongoing dialogue at group and country levels through due diligence and materiality assessments informs strategy and business model.

nodes.title: Interests and views of stakeholders
nodes.heading: Interests and views of stakeholders (1.3.2)
nodes.start_phrase:
Our stakeholders can be divided into two groups: affected stakeholders (those whose interests are affected or could be 
affected by our activities and business relationships across our value chain) and users/readers of the Sustainability Statement.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and approach: KBC Group describes how it creates sustainable value and considers environmental and social impacts across its entire value chain, leveraging its workforce, distribution networks, stakeholder relations, and financial capital. It references its business model (not externally assured).

- Value chain mapping: Outlines upstream activities (ICT, services, facilities), core own-operations enablers (human resources, infrastructure, sales/marketing, product development, business conduct), and downstream offerings (lending, asset management/investments, re/insurance, other financial and non-financial services). Communities where KBC operates are explicitly included.

- Stakeholder universe: Distinguishes affected stakeholders (clients, employees, suppliers, society at large, with nature as a “silent stakeholder”) from users/readers of the Sustainability Statement (investors, core shareholders, public authorities, business partners, unions, NGOs, governments, academics, analysts).

- Stakeholder engagement and interests: Details channels and expectations for:
  - Consumers: NPS, panels, local contacts, complaints; priorities include trust, privacy/cybersecurity, transparency, accessibility, expertise, innovation, simple/relevant solutions, personal advice.
  - Employees: Surveys, works councils, H&S committees, regular meetings; priorities include work-life balance, development, health and safety, ethical conduct.
  - Suppliers: ESG questionnaires, vendor meetings, transparent sourcing; seek transparency, collaboration, long-term ties, shared vision/risks/rewards, joint value, timely payment, contract respect.
  - Investors/core shareholders: Meetings, AGM, ratings and sustainability assessments (e.g., S&P CSA, CDP, Sustainalytics), ESG questionnaires; expect value creation, long-term model with clear financial/non-financial targets, ESG integration, transparency.
  - Public authorities: Sector federations, representative bodies, consultations, networking; focus on legal compliance.
  - Society: Works councils, sustainability networks, research/media, external academic advisory boards; focus on local employment, transparency, good communication.

- Governance integration: Executive Committee and Board are informed of engagement outcomes; inputs feed the KBC Sustainability Dashboard and materiality assessment, shaping strategy and the business model.

- Materiality and ESRS alignment: Identifies actual and potential impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) across own operations, upstream, and downstream, linked to ESRS sustainability matters including climate change (mitigation, energy, adaptation), water and marine resources, biodiversity and ecosystems, own workforce (working conditions, equal opportunities), privacy, consumers/end-users (information incl. cybersecurity, social inclusion), and business conduct (ethics/culture, supplier relationships).

- Climate change focus:
  - Impacts/opportunities: Downstream financing, investing, and insuring can negatively impact climate via exposure to carbon-intensive sectors, but also enable positive impact by funding renewable energy, low-carbon solutions, and tailored insurance products; retail awareness initiatives steer greener choices. Upstream influence includes encouraging supplier GHG reductions and renewable energy use, notably in automotive for leasing. Time horizons: climate impacts predominantly medium term; energy consumption/production short to medium term.
  - Risks: Transition risks (policy, technology, market shifts) and physical risks (temperature, water, wind, mass-related events) affect lending, insurance, and investments, creating financial risks (credit, market, liquidity, technical insurance) and non-financial risks (operational, reputational, compliance). Examples include asset repricing, volatility, credit losses, and climate litigation in the near to long term; increased insurance claims and asset/collateral devaluation in the medium to long term.

nodes.title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with strategy and business model
nodes.heading: Material impacts, risks and opportunities and their interaction with strategy and business model (1.3.3)
nodes.start_phrase:
During our materiality assessment, we identified actual and potential impacts, risks and opportunities associated with our own 
operations, and upstream and downstream value chain.
nodes.summary:
- The section outlines KBC Group’s material impacts, risks and opportunities across its own operations, upstream suppliers and downstream clients, aligned with ESRS topics and based on a materiality assessment.
- A matrix maps where impacts, risks and opportunities arise for key sustainability matters: climate change (mitigation, energy, adaptation), water and marine resources, biodiversity, own workforce (working conditions, equal treatment), privacy, consumers and end-users (information/cybersecurity, social inclusion), and business conduct (ethics/culture, supplier relationships).
- Climate change impacts are most material in the downstream value chain: potential negatives from financing or insuring carbon‑intensive activities; positives from lending/leasing for low‑carbon solutions, investing (own and client assets) in transition-enabling companies, climate-supportive insurance products, and steering retail clients toward greener choices.
- Upstream, KBC influences suppliers—especially in automotive leasing—to cut GHG emissions and adopt renewable energy.
- Time horizons: climate change impacts are mainly medium term; energy consumption/production impacts are short to medium term.
- Climate-related risks arise primarily through lending, insurance and investments, comprising transition risks (linked to mitigation and energy) and physical risks (linked to adaptation, driven by temperature, water, wind or mass-movement events).
- These risks can translate into financial (credit, market, liquidity, technical insurance) and non-financial (operational, reputational, compliance) exposures, including asset repricing, market volatility, credit losses, climate litigation, higher insurance claims, and reduced asset/collateral values over the medium to long term.

nodes.title: Overview of material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: Overview of material impacts, risks and opportunities (1.3.3.1)
nodes.start_phrase:
During our materiality assessment, we identified actual and potential impacts, risks and opportunities associated with our own 
operations, and upstream and downstream value chain.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and method: KBC Group’s 2024 ESRS-aligned materiality assessment identifies actual and potential impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) across the value chain (own operations, upstream, downstream), mapped to ESRS sustainability matters.
- Material topics and value-chain location: Climate change (mitigation/energy, adaptation), water and marine resources, biodiversity and ecosystems, own workforce (working conditions, equal treatment), consumers and end-users (information quality, privacy/cybersecurity, social inclusion), and business conduct (ethics, corporate culture, supplier relationships). A table links where impacts, risks and opportunities arise (OO/US/DS).
- Climate change:
  - Impacts: Downstream negatives from financing/insuring carbon-intensive activities; positives via lending, leasing and investing in renewables/low-carbon solutions; insurance products supporting transition; nudging retail demand to greener options; upstream supplier decarbonization (notably auto/leasing).
  - Risks: Material transition and physical risks creating financial (credit, market, liquidity, insurance) and non-financial (operational, reputational, compliance) risks over short/medium/long term (e.g., asset repricing, credit losses, higher claims).
  - Opportunities: Short-term opportunities supporting client transitions in housing, mobility, alternative energy (incl. storage) and new insurance offerings.
- Water and marine resources:
  - Risks: Transition risks from regulation reallocating water; physical risks from scarcity causing supply chain, water/food insecurity; medium/long-term financial effects.
  - Opportunities: Short-term financing of water treatment/saving solutions, incl. agriculture.
- Biodiversity and ecosystems:
  - Impacts: Not material for own operations; material via lending/investing in medium term; negatives from funding unsustainable land use; positives via investing in companies addressing resource scarcity.
  - Risks: Transition risks (e.g., anti-deforestation policies) and physical/systemic risks (supply disruptions, pandemic, food insecurity) affecting portfolios.
- Own workforce:
  - Impacts: Positive across working conditions, equal pay and opportunity, diversity & inclusion, anti-harassment, training, and strong privacy protection.
  - Risks: Reputational/litigation risk if employee privacy is breached (e.g., cyberattack); other labor risks deemed improbable; no material opportunities identified; transition plans have no material workforce impact.
- Consumers and end-users:
  - Impacts: Client-centric digital model considers privacy, quality of information, responsible marketing, and cybersecurity; special safeguards for children; positives from client cyber-awareness initiatives and financial/health data protection.
  - Risks: Short/medium/long-term operational, reputational, compliance risks from cyber/data/information issues and social exclusion; downstream credit risk if corporate clients mishandle social topics; third-party data loss risk mitigated via strong supplier controls.
  - Opportunities: Short-term advisory and information services guiding clients on sustainability (subsidies, regulations, taxonomy).
- Business conduct:
  - Impacts: Promote ethical culture; policies against tax avoidance; strong controls on AML/CTF, bribery/corruption, whistleblowing.
  - Risks: Legal/compliance, credit and operational risks if conduct policies fail across value chain; supplier-related risks (e.g., payment practices, corruption exposure).
- Changes and entity-specific notes: First ESRS sustainability statement—no prior-period changes to report; cybersecurity and responsible tax practices considered insufficiently covered by ESRS, so elaborated in Consumers (3.2) and Business conduct (4.1).
- Interaction with strategy and business model:
  - KBC integrates material environmental IROs into strategies, policies and actions (climate in 2.2.2, biodiversity in 2.4.2); environmental risk management embedded in the Risk Management Framework.
  - Client trust and centricity anchor the business model; strong focus on consumer/investor/data protection and information security to mitigate cyber impacts.
  - Workforce strategy emphasizes attraction/retention, trust, satisfaction, and privacy to enable execution.
  - Ethical business conduct and responsible behavior are foundational, with ongoing culture-building and monitoring of conduct risks.

nodes.title: Interaction with strategy and business model
nodes.heading: Interaction with strategy and business model (1.3.3.2)
nodes.start_phrase:
At KBC, we strive to create value for all our stakeholders through our financial products and services, including the society at 
large.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on business conduct: KBC aims to foster an ethical, responsible corporate culture across operations, with strict rules on responsible tax practices, anti-bribery/corruption, AML/CFT, whistle-blowing, and supplier conduct to mitigate legal, compliance, credit, and operational risks across its value chain.
- ESRS context: As KBC’s first sustainability statement under ESRS, no changes to material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) versus prior periods are disclosed. Entity-specific gaps noted—cybersecurity and responsible tax practices—are integrated into relevant sections.
- Strategy and business model: Client trust and centricity underpin the bank-insurer model, with strong consumer/investor/data protection, responsible marketing, and an Information Security Strategy to counter cybercrime. KBC supports client financial resilience and protects employee privacy, prioritising attraction, retention, and engagement of staff.
- Environmental integration: Climate and biodiversity strategies translate into policies and actions; environmental risk management (climate, water/marine, biodiversity) is embedded in the Risk Management Framework.
- Resilience and planning: Sustainability is embedded in annual financial planning, including climate targets, opportunity detection, and ESG risk in risk appetite. KBC pursues diversification and long-term stability over short-term gains.
- Scenario analysis and stress testing: Regular climate-related stress tests (transition and physical risks) across banking and insurance activities, alongside ICAAP/ILAAP/ORSA processes, indicate no material short-term impact and adequate capital/liquidity; long-term stability is not jeopardised, though portfolios and policies are being proactively adjusted for medium/long-term climate risks.
- Current financial effects: Due to data constraints and evolving ESG methodologies, precise quantification is limited; however, no material impact on consolidated financials is expected within the next reporting period.
- Double materiality assessment: Conducted per ESRS and EFRAG guidance with defined scoring and thresholds; risks rely on existing risk tools plus expert judgement; opportunities assessed via similar scoring. Annual review planned.
- Impact materiality process: Mapped value chain to distinguish direct and indirect impacts, especially from lending, investment, and insurance. Stakeholder engagement (surveys, dialogues, client meetings) and internal expert input informed the assessment.
- Tools and standards used: UNEP FI impact tools and internal White Papers for lending; Equator Principles for project finance (including community consultation and grievance mechanisms); responsible investing methodology for portfolios; engagement with an external Sustainability Board (ESB) and use of external sources (sector bodies, ESG ratings, GRI, SASB, peer reviews).

structure.title: Impact, risk and opportunity
structure.heading: Impact, risk and opportunity (1.4)
structure.start_phrase: Our double materiality assessment forms the foundation of this Sustainability Statement.
structure.summary:
- Explains KBC Group’s double materiality assessment underpinning the Sustainability Statement, covering both impact materiality (effects on society and environment) and financial materiality (sustainability-driven risks and opportunities for KBC).
- Describes alignment with ESRS and EFRAG Materiality Assessment Implementation Guidance, including a defined scoring method and quantitative thresholds based on a five-point scale from Minimal to Critical.
- Outlines how material risks are identified primarily via existing risk tools and assessments, supplemented by expert judgement; opportunities are scored using a mechanism similar to risk scoring.
- Notes this is the first application of the current double materiality approach in 2024, with plans for annual review and updates.
- Details the impact materiality process: early mapping of value-chain business relationships and geographies to distinguish own-operations impacts from indirect impacts through lending, investment, and insurance activities.
- Highlights extensive stakeholder engagement (surveys, dialogues, client meetings) and input from internal experts to identify environmental, social, and governance impacts.
- Specifies use of UNEP FI impact identification tools and KBC strategic White Papers for lending portfolio impacts.
- Confirms adoption of the Equator Principles for major project finance and advisory, including community consultation and grievance mechanisms.
- Describes responsible investing methodology for investment portfolios, assessing companies’ sustainability characteristics and turnover share from sustainable activities.
- Notes engagement with an external expert Sustainability Board (ESB) and use of external references (sector bodies, S&P Global ESG Materiality Maps, ESG rating agencies, and frameworks like GRI and SASB), plus peer insights.

nodes.title: Description of the processes to identify and assess material impact, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: Description of the processes to identify and assess material impact, risks and opportunities (1.4.1)
nodes.start_phrase: Our double materiality assessment forms the foundation of this Sustainability Statement.
nodes.summary:
- Explains KBC Group’s double materiality assessment, aligning with ESRS and EFRAG guidance, including scoring methods, thresholds, and annual review intent.
- Details impact materiality: mapping value chain to distinguish own operations vs. indirect portfolio impacts; broad stakeholder engagement; use of UNEP FI tools, Equator Principles, responsible investing methodology, and external sources; desktop synthesis of potential topics.
- Highlights climate impact findings: Scope 3 Category 15 (portfolio) emissions are most material; references to related targets and inventories. Biodiversity review finds no direct site impacts from offices; main biodiversity impacts via lending/investments assessed with ENCORE, with highest-impact sectors (building/construction, agriculture, energy) and key drivers (land, water, marine use).
- Describes impact scoring process: internal experts and senior leadership assess scale, scope, likelihood, and irremediability across time horizons, for own operations and value chain, classifying impacts on a five-point scale.
- Outlines financial materiality of risks: ESG risks embedded across traditional risk types; aggregation of matters for meaningful assessment; likelihood and financial effect scored on four-point scales per risk type and integrated via thresholds.
- Presents ERIM as core tool for environmental risk identification: transition and physical risks for climate, biodiversity, water, pollution, and circularity; three time horizons and NGFS scenarios (Orderly 1.5°C, Disorderly 2°C, Hot House ~3°C); country-specific analyses; deep dives using PACTA, sector reporting, and hazard mapping (floods, heat, drought, wildfires, windstorms, landslides, subsidence, erosion).
- Covers opportunities: identified by experts across the value chain and time horizons; assessed on likelihood and financial magnitude; focus on embedding opportunities into core products/services and White Paper sector cycles; integration into annual budgeting, with recognition that opportunity management is less mature than impacts/risks.
- Summarizes governance and decision-making: iterative reviews by Group Corporate Sustainability; HR validation for workforce impacts; approvals by CSRD Steering Committee, risk management, and European Works Council; cross-functional working group oversight.
- Provides an index of ESRS disclosure requirements covered and where they appear in the Sustainability Statement, including general disclosures and topic-specific E1–E4 items (climate, pollution, water/marine, biodiversity).

nodes.title: Disclosure requirements in ESRS covered by the undertaking’s sustainability statement
nodes.heading: Disclosure requirements in ESRS covered by the undertaking’s sustainability statement (1.4.2)
nodes.start_phrase: Below, we have listed all disclosure requirements covered in this Sustainability Statement.
nodes.summary:
- Context and purpose: Extract from KBC Group’s 2024 Annual Report outlining which ESRS disclosure requirements are covered in the Sustainability Statement and where each appears in the report.
- Materiality approach: States that KBC performed expert-based evaluations to determine which underlying information requirements are material, considering significance and user decision-making needs.
- ESRS 2 general disclosures: Cross-references to sections covering basis of preparation, special circumstances, governance roles and oversight, integration of sustainability into incentives, due diligence, internal controls over sustainability reporting, strategy/business model/value chain, stakeholder interests, material impacts/risks/opportunities (IRO), and the processes used to identify and assess them.
- Environmental topical standards:
  - Climate (E1): Transition plan, policies, actions/resources, targets, gross Scope 1–3 and total GHG emissions, GHG removals/credits, internal carbon pricing, and related ESRS 2 links.
  - Pollution (E2): Processes to identify and assess pollution-related impacts/risks/opportunities.
  - Water and marine resources (E3): Policies, actions/resources, and targets.
  - Biodiversity and ecosystems (E4): Integration into strategy and business model, policies, actions/resources, and targets.
  - Resource use and circular economy (E5): Processes to identify and assess related impacts/risks/opportunities.
- Social topical standards:
  - Own workforce (S1): Policies; worker engagement; grievance/remediation channels; actions and mitigation; targets; workforce characteristics; collective bargaining; diversity; adequate wages; health & safety metrics; pay gap/total remuneration; incidents/complaints and severe human rights impacts.
  - Consumers and end-users (S4): Policies; engagement; remediation channels; actions/risks/opportunities and effectiveness; targets.
- Governance topical standard:
  - Business conduct (G1): Policies and culture; supplier relationship management; minimum disclosure on actions; anti-corruption/bribery prevention and detection; incidents; payment practices.
- Mapping to other EU legislation: Detailed table linking ESRS datapoints to SFDR Principal Adverse Impact indicators, CRR/Pillar 3 ESG disclosure templates (EU 2022/2453), Benchmark Regulation (EU 2020/1818), EU Climate Law (EU 2021/1119), and Delegated Regulations (EU 2020/1816), with precise report section references and flags for Not applicable, Not material, or Subject to phase-in.
- Illustrative datapoints in the mapping: Board gender diversity and independence, due diligence statements, involvement in fossil fuels/chemicals/controversial weapons/tobacco, climate neutrality transition plan and benchmark exclusions, GHG reduction targets and intensities, energy consumption/intensity, climate physical risk exposure and EPC breakdown of real estate, pollutant emissions, water metrics, biodiversity/deforestation policies, forced/child labour risk, fatalities/accidents and days lost, gender pay gap and CEO pay ratio, discrimination incidents, anti-corruption fines and standards, whistleblower protections.
- Applicability/materiality notes: Several E1 energy metrics, E2 pollution releases, E3 water reuse/consumption, E5 waste, and multiple S2/S3 value chain human rights datapoints are assessed as Not material; certain climate physical risk and real estate energy efficiency disclosures are Subject to phase-in; some governance datapoints are Not applicable.
- Environmental information (EU Taxonomy Article 8): Introduces taxonomy disclosures and explains conditions for taxonomy alignment (eligibility via Delegated Acts, substantial contribution and do-no-significant-harm criteria, and minimum social/governance safeguards), and begins listing the six environmental objectives (including climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources, and transition to a circular economy).

structure.title: Environmental information
structure.heading: Environmental information
structure.start_phrase: The Taxonomy Regulation establishes an EU-wide framework according to which investors and businesses can assess whether certain economic activities are environmentally sustainable.
structure.summary: The excerpt from KBC Group’s 2024 Annual Report outlines environmental disclosures under Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation. It explains the criteria for an economic activity to be considered taxonomy-aligned: being a taxonomy-eligible activity listed in Delegated Acts, meeting Technical Screening Criteria for substantial contribution and do-no-significant-harm, and complying with minimum social and governance safeguards. It introduces the EU Taxonomy’s six environmental objectives and explicitly lists four of them: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources, and transition to a circular economy. The section sets the framework for how KBC assesses and reports on the environmental sustainability of its activities.

nodes.title: Disclosures pursuant to Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852 (Taxonomy Regulation)
nodes.heading: Disclosures pursuant to Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852 (Taxonomy Regulation) (2.1)
nodes.start_phrase: The Taxonomy Regulation establishes an EU-wide framework according to which investors and businesses can assess whether certain economic activities are environmentally sustainable.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: KBC Group’s 2024 environmental information discloses EU Taxonomy Article 8 metrics under the Disclosure Delegated Act (DDA) for its activities as a credit institution, insurer/reinsurer, and asset manager. It explains the Taxonomy’s criteria (eligibility, substantial contribution with DNSH, and minimum safeguards) and its six environmental objectives.
- Data challenges: Persistent data gaps due to the European Single Access Point not yet operational, many counterparties not yet subject to CSRD (hence no Taxonomy reporting), and insufficient asset-level data for household mortgages and vehicle loans (e.g., building characteristics, EV tyres/circularity). KBC also publishes voluntary, approximation-based Taxonomy percentages in its Sustainability Report; the annual report focuses on mandatory disclosures.
- Methodology notes: Detailed DDA tables are available in the Additional information section; where required, KPIs are calculated on both counterparty Turnover and CapEx, with narrative discussion limited to Turnover-based KPIs. Certain exposures (e.g., trading portfolio, central banks/governments) are excluded where prescribed.
- Credit institution (GAR): Mandatory eligibility of assets at 41.0% (40.8% in 2023). Alignment (Green Asset Ratio) at 0.5% (0.2% in 2023), with improvement driven by treating CSRD subsidiaries/SPVs as CSRD entities and better counterparty information. Ratios remain low due to data limitations and asymmetric numerator/denominator definitions; denominator includes non-CSRD counterparties and non-eligible assets (e.g., derivatives, cash, goodwill). Off-balance financial guarantees alignment is 1.4% (0.4% in 2023).
- Insurer/reinsurer underwriting KPI: Percentages based on gross written premiums in non-life. Eligibility at 12.5% (14.3% in 2023), tied to coverage of climate-related perils in motor and property lines. Alignment at 1.7%, now limited to the Belgian corporate “fire and other property damage” portfolio. Decline from 6.6% (2023) reflects methodological refinements and a narrower interpretation of Taxonomy criteria, noting challenges for mass retail products to meet all technical screening criteria (e.g., risk-based incentives and preventive measures). Ongoing actions include integrating flood maps in underwriting and exploring incentives for policyholder risk prevention.
- Insurer/reinsurer investments (GIR): Eligibility at 14.8% (8.5% in 2023); alignment at 1.4% (0.5% in 2023), largely due to improved data availability. Investments are mainly managed by KBC Asset Management using an external data provider; amounts with central banks/governments are excluded.
- Asset manager KPI (DCM): Eligibility at 8.7% (2.0% in 2023); alignment at 1.8% (0.9% in 2023), primarily from better data coverage. Central bank/government exposures are excluded.
- Consolidated financial conglomerate KPIs (revenue-weighted): Credit institution GAR 0.5% (turnover-based) and 0.4% (capex-based); insurer combined 1.4%/1.5% (with underwriting 1.7%/1.7% and investments 1.4%/1.8%); asset manager 1.8%/2.6%; consolidated KPI 0.8%/0.9%.
- Climate strategy and transition planning: KBC has embedded key transition plan elements (governance, strategy, scenario analysis, risk/opportunity management, financial planning, target setting, engagement) into its sustainability governance and business strategy, though not yet consolidated into a single formal plan. Oversight lies with the Sustainable Finance Steering Committee, ISB, ExCo, and Board; implementation is coordinated via a Sustainable Finance Programme and a Data and Metrics Steering Programme.
- Targets and monitoring: Targets address own operations and material financed/invested emissions, with several aligned to a 1.5°C pathway. Progress is reported semi-annually to top governance via a Sustainability Dashboard covering key metrics, decarbonisation levers, and actions. Climate is integrated into financial planning and budgeting (e.g., macro scenarios, volume/target tracking, risk profile impacts), with KBC reporting it is broadly on track.
- Risk and opportunity management: ESG/climate risks are embedded in the Risk Management Framework. Sectoral/thematic “White Papers” and tailored assessments identify risks and opportunities, inform product development and client engagement for transition support, and feed into financial planning (portfolio mix, expenses, capital adequacy). Regular monitoring and management reporting ensure transparency and accountability.

nodes.title: Climate change
nodes.heading: Climate change (2.2)
nodes.start_phrase: In an initial phase, KBC has focused on several important pillars in order to embed climate transition plan elements within its overall sustainability governance and strategy but has so far not formalised these into an integrated single document.
nodes.summary:
- KBC has embedded climate transition planning elements into overall sustainability governance and strategy but has not yet formalized them into a single integrated transition plan; no decision yet on if/when such a plan will be adopted.
- Current transition planning pillars: Governance, Strategy, Scenario analysis, Risk and opportunity management, Financial planning, Target setting, and Engagement.
- Governance structure involves the Sustainable Finance Steering Committee, ISB, ExCo, and the Board, which oversee environmental issues, integrate them into business strategy, and approve climate strategy and targets.
- Dedicated programs support implementation and data: a Sustainable Finance Programme and a Data and Metrics Steering Programme with its own Steering Committee.
- Climate targets cover own operations and material financed/invested emissions; some align with 1.5°C pathways, making the approach partly 1.5°C-aligned.
- Progress and actions are reported semi-annually to top governance bodies via a Sustainability Dashboard tracking key targets, decarbonisation levers, and actions.
- Financial planning integrates climate considerations: inclusion in macroeconomic scenarios for budgeting, monitoring of climate-related volumes/targets, and assessment of climate risk impacts on the risk profile.
- KBC reports being broadly on track to meet climate targets and continues implementing key actions.
- Climate-related risks and opportunities are identified through sectoral/thematic “White Papers” and tailored assessments; ESG risk (including climate) is embedded across the Risk Management Framework.
- Findings translate into client engagement, support for client transition, development of sustainable products, and monitoring of decarbonisation progress.
- Outcomes feed into climate strategy, target follow-up, and financial planning, influencing portfolio mix, expenses, and capital adequacy.
- Regular monitoring and management reporting ensure transparency and accountability for stakeholders to track progress and effectiveness.

nodes.title: Climate change strategy
nodes.heading: Climate change strategy (2.2.1)
nodes.start_phrase: In an initial phase, KBC has focused on several important pillars in order to embed climate transition plan elements within its overall sustainability governance and strategy but has so far not formalised these into an integrated single document.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: KBC Group’s climate change transition planning approach within its 2024 Annual Report (section 2.2.1.1), noting no single integrated transition plan has been formalized yet and no adoption timeline decided.
- Embedded pillars of transition planning: Governance, Strategy, Scenario analysis, Risk and opportunity management, Financial planning, Target setting, and Engagement.
- Governance and oversight: Sustainable Finance Steering Committee, ISB, ExCo, and Board oversee environmental issues, climate strategy, and targets; a Sustainable Finance Programme coordinates implementation; a Data and Metrics Steering Programme manages climate data and reporting.
- Targets and alignment: Targets cover own operations and material financed/invested emissions; some are aligned with 1.5°C pathways, making the current approach partly 1.5°C-aligned.
- Monitoring and reporting: Biannual reporting to ISB, ExCo, and Board via a Sustainability Dashboard tracking progress, KPIs, decarbonisation levers, and actions; overall progress is on track.
- Integration into financial planning: Climate integrated into budgeting through Chief Economist scenarios; follow-up on climate-related volumes/targets; climate risk impacts considered in the risk profile.
- Risk and opportunity management: Identified via sectoral/thematic White Papers and tailored assessments; ESG risks embedded in the Risk Management Framework; opportunities translated into products/services; client engagement supports transition and decarbonisation monitoring.
- Link to business outcomes: Insights feed into climate strategy, target follow-up, portfolio mix, expenses, and capital adequacy; regular monitoring and management reporting ensure transparency and accountability.

nodes.title: Transition plan for climate change mitigation
nodes.heading: Transition plan for climate change mitigation (2.2.1.1)
nodes.start_phrase: In an initial phase, KBC has focused on several important pillars in order to embed climate transition plan elements within its overall sustainability governance and strategy but has so far not formalised these into an integrated single document.
nodes.summary:
- KBC has not yet consolidated its climate transition plan into a single integrated document, but has embedded key elements across seven pillars: governance, strategy, scenario analysis, risk and opportunity management, financial planning, target setting, and engagement.
- Strong governance oversees climate strategy via the Sustainable Finance Steering Committee, ISB, ExCo and Board; a Sustainable Finance Programme coordinates implementation, and a Data and Metrics Steering Programme manages climate data and reporting.
- Climate targets cover both own operations and material financed/invested emissions; several are aligned with 1.5°C pathways, making the current approach partly 1.5°C-aligned.
- Progress on targets and actions is tracked biannually through a Sustainability Dashboard reported to top governance bodies; decarbonisation levers and actions are monitored.
- Climate considerations are embedded in annual financial planning, including macroeconomic scenarios, tracking of climate-related business volumes, and integration of climate risk into the risk profile.
- Climate-related risks and opportunities are identified via sectoral/thematic White Papers and tailored assessments; ESG risk is integrated across the Risk Management Framework; outcomes influence strategy, product development, client engagement, portfolio mix, expenses, and capital adequacy.
- Scenario analysis uses IEA, NGFS, and customised scenarios (including 1.5°C pathways) to inform risk identification, strategic planning, resilience assessments, target setting, and capacity building.
- Stakeholder engagement includes policymakers and clients to amplify transition impacts and share best practices.
- No locked-in emissions in own operations have been identified that would jeopardise GHG targets; lending targets in high-emitting sectors support decarbonisation and help mitigate stranded-asset risk; potential locked-in emissions are not quantified but are monitored through target updates and White Papers.
- KBC confirms it does not trigger the exclusion criteria of Articles 12.1 and 12.2 of the EU Climate Benchmark Regulation (EU 2020/1818).
- A consolidated Sustainability Policy Framework sets out scope, governance, and policies combining exclusions and conditional criteria; it applies globally to core (lending, insurance, advisory, investment advice) and supporting activities (own investments, procurement).
- The framework covers controversial sectors/issues (e.g., human rights, energy, steel, cement and aluminium, mining, defence, biodiversity, gambling, tobacco, animal-related activities, prostitution), enforces due diligence and expert review (including reputational risk), and is updated at least biennially with internal and external stakeholder input (ISB and ESB).

nodes.title: Climate change: Impact, risk and opportunity management
nodes.heading: Climate change: Impact, risk and opportunity management (2.2.2)
nodes.start_phrase: All sustainability-related policies are bundled in our Sustainability Policy Framework, offering a condensed but comprehensive overview of these policies.
nodes.summary:
- KBC uses multiple climate scenarios (IEA, NGFS, and custom) covering varied models, timeframes, temperature goals including 1.5°C, and regions to inform risk identification, resilience analysis, strategy, financial planning, target setting, capacity building, and risk/opportunity management.
- The group engages policymakers and clients to spread best practices and extend positive impacts beyond its own operations.
- No locked-in emissions have been identified in own operations that would jeopardize GHG reduction targets; climate-related lending targets drive decarbonization in high-emitting sectors and help mitigate stranded asset risk. Potential locked-in emissions are not quantified, but potential stranded assets are monitored via target progress and White Paper reviews.
- KBC confirms that none of the exclusion criteria of the EU Climate Benchmark Regulation (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/1818) apply.
- The document outlines climate change impact, risk and opportunity management (2.2.2) and details policies on mitigation and adaptation (2.2.2.1).
- A comprehensive Sustainability Policy Framework consolidates policies, defines scope and governance, combines exclusions and conditional criteria, and applies globally across lending, insurance, advisory, investment advice, own investments, and procurement. It covers sensitive sectors (e.g., human rights, energy, metals, mining, defense, biodiversity, gambling, tobacco, animal-related activities, prostitution), is enforced via strict due diligence with expert input and reputational risk review, updated at least biennially, and overseen by internal (ISB) and external stakeholder (ESB) bodies.

nodes.title: Policies related to climate change mitigation and adaptation
nodes.heading: Policies related to climate change mitigation and adaptation (2.2.2.1)
nodes.start_phrase: All sustainability-related policies are bundled in our Sustainability Policy Framework, offering a condensed but comprehensive overview of these policies.
nodes.summary:
- Uses multiple climate scenarios (IEA, NGFS, and custom) across models, time horizons, temperature pathways (including 1.5°C), and regions to inform risk identification, strategy, resilience, financial planning, target setting, capacity building, and risk/opportunity management.
- Engages policymakers and clients to amplify transition impact; reports no locked-in emissions jeopardizing own-operations GHG targets; employs climate lending targets to decarbonize high-emitting sectors and mitigate stranded asset risk; complies with EU Climate Benchmark Regulation Articles 12.1 and 12.2.
- Sustainability Policy Framework consolidates policies, sets scope and governance (ISB, ESB, ExCo), embeds due diligence and reputational risk assessment, applies group-wide to core and supporting activities, covers controversial sectors (e.g., energy, mining, metals, defence, biodiversity, gambling, tobacco, animal-related, prostitution), and is updated at least biennially.
- Environmental Policy commits to supporting a low‑carbon, climate‑resilient society by:
  - Developing products/services that enable the transition.
  - Reducing environmental/climate impact across loans, investments, insurance, and advice.
  - Raising internal/external awareness and engaging suppliers.
  - Supported by a group sustainability team (challenge business, review policies, provide implementation guidance) and aligned with Paris Agreement, TCFD, GHG Protocol, CCCA, UNEP FI PRB; addresses mitigation, adaptation, energy efficiency, and renewable deployment.
- Energy Policy aligns with the Paris goals via CCCA; excludes financing/insurance/advisory for thermal coal projects and imposes strict conditions on companies still involved in coal; excludes exploration/development of unconventional oil and gas and any new oil/gas fields; globally applies to electricity/heat generation and related suppliers; prioritizes the shift to renewables.
- Recalculation Policy defines when and how to restate base-year emissions for own and financed emissions targets, with decisions by ISB or delegated committee; based on GHG Protocol; ensures disclosure to external assurance providers as needed.
- Investment Policy (all investments, worldwide) excludes issuers on KBC Blacklist/Human Rights Offenders/Controversial Regimes, thermal coal extraction/coal power, and tobacco; integrates into KBC AM processes; supports mitigation/renewables by excluding high-negative-impact activities.
- Responsible Investing funds policy (SFDR Article 8/9) applies negative screening plus positive selection; sets portfolio targets (ESG risk scores, GHG emissions, green/social/sustainability bonds, sustainable investments); conducts proxy voting and engagement; governed by KBC AM with ISB review; aligned with the Towards Sustainability label; annually reviewed.
- Exclusion Policy for Responsible Investing funds specifies negative screens: fossil fuels, tobacco, arms, gambling, adult entertainment; bans instruments linked to livestock/food prices; restricts fur/special leather; excludes countries with unfair tax practices or severe ESG violations; with governance and stakeholder oversight.
- Actions and resources: via the Sustainable Finance Programme (expanded in 2022 to biodiversity and water) KBC manages own footprint by implementing ISO 14001 in core countries, reducing energy and sourcing/producing renewable energy, leveraging renovations/relocations, promoting greener mobility (telework, cycling, public transport, electrified fleet), and cutting waste/paper/water; examples include replacing cooling with heat pumps in Belgium and reusing server-room heat with heat pumps in Prague HQ.

nodes.title: Actions and resources in relation to climate change policies
nodes.heading: Actions and resources in relation to climate change policies (2.2.2.2)
nodes.start_phrase: In addition to having policies in place to prevent, mitigate and remediate actual and potential impacts, and to address risks, we also take numerous measures to put our commitment to climate into practice.
nodes.summary:
- Exclusion Policy for Responsible Investing Funds: Applies to all Responsible Investing funds managed by KBC Asset Management subsidiaries; approved by KBC AM ExCo, reviewed by the ISB, with implementation accountability at the Financial Risk Committee. Aligns with the Towards Sustainability Labelling Agency standards and was consulted with the external Responsible Investing Advisory Board. Focuses on climate mitigation and renewable energy by excluding fossil fuel-involved issuers.

- Sustainable Finance Programme and climate actions: Group-wide programme started in 2019 (expanded in 2022 to biodiversity and water) translating climate commitments into practice. Measures include ISO 14001 in core countries, energy reduction and switch to renewables, building renovations, greener mobility (telework, bikes, public transport, EV fleet), and resource reduction (waste, paper, water). Examples include heat pump deployments and heat recovery.

- Managing own operational footprint: Full-group GHG inventory with annual actions toward long-term targets. Decarbonisation levers include energy efficiency, renewable energy sourcing and self-generation, and low-carbon transport. Integration into regular operations with clear follow-up.

- Loan portfolio decarbonisation: Annual calculation of portfolio emissions across all lending and leasing; key actions include financing zero/low-carbon solutions, supporting client transition (e.g., renovation loans), or exiting relationships. Targets extend to 2050 with 2030 milestones across sectors (energy incl. thermal coal, vehicles, buildings, agriculture, cement, steel, aluminium). Success depends on supportive public policy.

- Continuous GHG target monitoring for Responsible funds: Daily monitoring of weighted average GHG intensity at portfolio level; funds must maintain a path to a 50% reduction by 2030 after an initial 30% cut, adjusting holdings as needed. Exclusions apply; achievement depends on issuer data updates.

- Monitoring KBC Insurance investment portfolio: Regular tracking of weighted average GHG intensity for corporate investments (bonds and listed equities; excluding unit-linked). Exclusion policy applies to new investments; managers can steer via emissions intensity within constraints.

- Climate White Papers: Ongoing, cyclical assessments across lending and insurance to evaluate environmental impacts, dependencies, risks and opportunities in selected sectors/themes. Outputs inform policies, targets, risk/opportunity management, and client engagement, aiming to stop financing harmful activities or support sector transitions. Dependent on Paris-aligned policy environments.

- Green bond issuance: Outstanding green bonds total 2.75 billion euros (two legacy bonds totaling 1.25 billion; a 750 million issue in 2021; and a 750 million issue in 2024). Updated framework (Nov 2023) aligns with ICMA Green Bond Principles 2021 and the EU Taxonomy. Eligible categories: energy-efficient residential/commercial buildings (Belgium), renewable energy (EU/UK), and zero-emission transport (Belgium). Annual impact reporting; future issuance planned; pipeline and policy incentives are key enablers.

- ESG risk integration in Risk Management Framework: ESG risks embedded across traditional risk types (credit, market, insurance, operational, reputational). Actions include:
  - Risk identification/materiality (ERIM, NAPP, sectoral E&S Heatmap, reputational ESG scores, ESG underwriting/outsourcing checks, and White Papers).
  - Measurement and stress testing (scenario analyses; integrating ESG drivers into stress tests).
  - Risk appetite with an explicit ESG objective across short-, medium-, and long-term horizons, supported by policies and targets.
  - Analysis, monitoring, and reporting via internal reports and dashboards to ExCo, RCC, and the Board.
  - Climate specifics: ERIM Impact Map, use of PACTA/TRUCOST/PCAF, physical risk assessments (e.g., flood, drought, heat, wildfires), climate scenarios in ICAAP/ILAAP/ORSA, and climate KRIs in a semiannual Board dashboard.

- New and Active Product Process (NAPP): Group-wide governance ensuring fair client outcomes, strategic fit, risk mitigation, and compliance for all products/services/changes. Mitigates ESG and greenwashing risks, with mandatory sustainability expert input for “green”-labelled products aligned to EU Taxonomy and ICMA, and ESG risk assessments by Risk and Compliance.

- Climate metrics and targets: Emphasis on reducing direct and indirect carbon footprint with defined targets for own operations, lending, and investment portfolios. Emission intensity metrics support transition risk monitoring and feed into the Climate Risk Dashboard. Own footprint covers Scope 1, 2, and 3 (including business/commuter travel and operational resources), with financed emissions (Scope 3 Cat. 15) acknowledged as most significant. Targets are endorsed by ISB, ExCo, and the Board, with supplier engagement via the Sustainability Code of Conduct.

nodes.title: Climate change metrics and targets
nodes.heading: Climate change metrics and targets (2.2.3)
nodes.start_phrase: We focus on diminishing our negative impact on climate change through the reduction of our direct and indirect carbon footprint.
nodes.summary:

nodes.title: Targets related to climate change mitigation and adaptation
