nodes.title: Own carbon footprint targets
nodes.heading: Own carbon footprint targets (2.2.3.1.1)
nodes.start_phrase: The ambition to reduce our negative impact on the environment is stipulated as a key objective in the Environmental Policy.
nodes.summary:
- Section focus: KBC Group’s climate change metrics and targets, used to mitigate and adapt to climate change and to monitor transition, credit and reputational risks via a Climate Risk Dashboard.
- Target scope: Separate targets for (i) own carbon footprint, (ii) loan and lease portfolios, and (iii) investment portfolios.
- Own carbon footprint definitions:
  - Scope 1: direct emissions from buildings and company-owned car fleet.
  - Scope 2: indirect emissions from purchased energy.
  - Scope 3: business and commuter travel and other operationally controlled sources (paper, water, waste). Notes that Scope 3 Category 15 (financed emissions) is most material for financial institutions.
- Governance and supplier engagement: Targets set with stakeholders in core countries; approved by ISB and ExCo and endorsed by the Board. Supplier alignment via Sustainability Code of Conduct.
- Own carbon footprint targets and status:
  - Base year 2015; GHG Protocol Corporate Standard applied.
  - Coverage: Scopes 1, 2 (market-based for monitoring) and selected Scope 3 categories (1, 5, 6, 7). Gases covered: CO2, CH4, N2O, PFCs, HFCs, SF6, NF3.
  - Reduction target: −80% by 2030 (annual linear 5.33%), 1.5°C-aligned per CDP guidance.
  - Offsetting: commitment to offset all remaining own emissions since 2021.
  - Renewable electricity: objective of 100% by 2030; methodology aligned with carbon footprint reporting; reported at 100% in 2024.
  - Progress: CO2e from own operations reduced from 170,735 tCO2e (2015) to 53,934 tCO2e (2024), a 68% cut; on track for 34,147 tCO2e by 2030. Building efficiency and fleet electrification contributing; commuter travel remains a challenge. Metrics receive reasonable assurance since 2016.
- Scope and boundary note: Targets cover all entities in financial consolidation within the bank-insurance context; GHG inventory also includes some entities outside that scope or not fully consolidated.
- Recalculation Policy (2023): Based on GHG Protocol; recalculation triggers include structural changes (M&A), methodology/assumption changes, and discovered errors; 5% threshold; data quality improvements excluded. FY2024 methodology updates were below threshold—no restatement needed.
- Loan and lease portfolio targets:
  - Framed by commitment to align with the Paris Agreement (well below 2°C, striving for 1.5°C).
  - Implemented through sectoral policies (e.g., bans on certain fossil fuel activities; stringent lending criteria for steel, cement, aluminium).
  - Policies and targets apply across all business units consistent with financial consolidation; governance approvals by ISB, ExCo, Board.
  - Target-setting incorporates core-country input, portfolio growth projections, and prevailing local regulations; achievement depends on timely government action and client engagement, especially in hard-to-abate sectors.

nodes.title: Loan and lease portfolio targets
nodes.heading: Loan and lease portfolio targets (2.2.3.1.2)
nodes.start_phrase: The environmental targets set on our lending portfolios must be understood in the overarching context of KBC’s commitment to align our activities with the Paris Agreement goal of limiting global warming to well below 2°C, striving for 1.5°C.
nodes.summary:
- Document context: Excerpts from KBC Group’s 2024 Annual Report detailing climate-related targets and progress for loan and lease portfolios (2.2.3.1.2) and asset management activities (2.2.3.1.3).

- Strategy and governance:
  - Commitment to align activities with the Paris Agreement (well below 2°C, striving for 1.5°C).
  - Sectoral policies restrict harmful activities (e.g., fossil fuels) and set strict lending criteria for steel, cement, aluminium.
  - Targets cover all business units within KBC’s consolidation scope; reviewed by ISB, ExCo, and endorsed by the Board.
  - Portfolio projections account for growth, local regulations, and client engagement; dependency on timely governmental action noted.

- Target framework and methodology:
  - Focus on sector-specific carbon intensity metrics (not absolute emissions); borrowers’ Scope 1 and, where applicable, Scope 2 included; Scope 3 excluded.
  - Use of PCAF methodologies/data and a Recalculation Policy to maintain boundary consistency.
  - Four-step science-based target-setting approach:
    1) Establish 2021 baselines using KBC portfolio data and climate-relevant data.
    2) Select credible climate scenarios (NGFS regional, EU PRIMES/MIX, IEA or other global) aligned with well-below 2°C/1.5°C pathways.
    3) Apply alignment methods: SDA/convergence for physical intensity; rate-of-reduction for agriculture (financial intensity).
    4) Project portfolio evolution using in-house views, company commitments, and proposed actions.
  - Non-scenario-based (partially science-based) financial intensity targets for the whole Energy sector and whole Real Estate sector.
  - Additional targets: complete phase-out of direct thermal coal financing (set 2016, achieved 2023); target for renewables’ share in energy lending (not science-based).
  - Monitoring based primarily on outstanding exposure; exceptions (cement, steel, aluminium) use granted exposure to reduce volatility.
  - No changes to targets/metrics/methodologies in 2024; annual monitoring; limited assurance on disclosed target metrics since 2021; formal review at least every five years.

- Portfolio targets and 2024 progress highlights (vs 2021 baselines):
  - Thermal coal: direct exposure reduced to zero (target achieved).
  - Energy:
    - Electricity GHG intensity down 56% (210 to 93 kg CO2e/MWh); on track.
    - Whole sector financial intensity down 42% (453 to 265 t CO2e/m EUR); on track.
    - Renewables’ share in total energy portfolio increased to 67.5% (target 75% by 2030); on track with potential volatility due to transition dynamics.
  - Real estate:
    - Residential real estate physical intensity down ~10% (not yet in line with 2024 pathway); improvement driven by better EPC labels and smaller average surfaces per € financed; further progress depends on government incentives.
    - Whole real estate sector financial intensity down 15% (27 to 23 t CO2e/m EUR); on track.
  - Transport:
    - Passenger car loans/financial leases: intensity down 11% (139 to 124 g CO2/km); on track.
    - Light commercial vehicle loans/financial leases: slight decrease (-1%; 208 to 205 g CO2/km); on track but slower due to limited electrified van availability.
    - Passenger car operational leasing: intensity down 42% (133 to 77 g CO2/km); on track.
    - LCV operational leasing: intensity down 5% (196 to 186 g CO2/km); on track.
    - Majority of newly financed vehicles are EVs; different adoption speeds across countries.
  - Agriculture: financial intensity down 25% (1,405 to 1,059 t CO2e/m EUR); on track. Changes influenced by PCAF standard updates (including emission factors/inflation adjustments), portfolio shifts, and data quality improvements; overall data quality remains a constraint.
  - Cement: intensity down 9% (0.69 to 0.62 t CO2e/t); on track; improvements reflect better data and client decarbonisation execution.
  - Steel: intensity up 12% (1.34 to 1.50 t CO2e/t); not on track; portfolio concentrated in one group facing delays in net-zero capex; ongoing client engagement.
  - Aluminium: intensity significantly reduced (0.59 to 0.21 t CO2e/t) and well below global sector benchmark; on track; reduction largely due to improved client data quality.

- Target-setting evidence and data quality:
  - Scenario references include NGFS, EU PRIMES/MIX, IEA ETP 2020 SDS, and TPI for aluminium; ambitions at well-below 2°C/1.5°C.
  - PCAF data quality scores disclosed (vary by sector); real estate calculations presently have high uncertainty; methodology and emission factors to be refined for 2025 disclosures.
  - External assurance: targets generally not externally assured; portfolio target metrics receive limited assurance.

- Asset management activities:
  - Objective: channel more client assets into Responsible Investing (RI) and align investing with the Paris Agreement; includes unit-linked assets managed by KBC Asset Management.
  - Governance: targets set by KBC Asset Management; approved by ISB, ExCo, and endorsed by the Board.
  - Targets and 2024 status:
    - Share of RI funds in total DCM: 33% (2021) to 44% (2024); 45% (2025) and 55% (2030) targets; on track.
    - Share of RI funds in total annual fund production (gross sales): 55% (2021) to 51% (2024); 65% (2025) target; on track.
    - Carbon intensity (Scope 1+2) of corporate investees in RI funds: 196 tCO2e/m USD revenue (2019) to 55 (2024 Q3), a 72% reduction vs a -50% 2030 target; on track.
  - Scope and methodology: RI funds pursue diverse sustainability objectives; climate mitigation is most common but not always primary. Carbon-intensity target covers corporate equities/bonds with Trucost data; ≥90% coverage of corporate investments; funds-of-funds excluded; Scope 3 excluded for consistency/comparability. Target ambition inspired by the Net Zero Asset Managers Initiative (not conclusive scientific evidence).
  - Monitoring: RI shares tracked monthly; carbon intensity monitored continuously; no target/methodology changes in 2024.

nodes.title: Asset management activities
nodes.heading: Asset management activities (2.2.3.1.3)
nodes.start_phrase: For our asset management activities, we also set and monitor climate-related targets.
nodes.summary:
- Context and sector updates: KBC flags delays in clients’ capital expenditure plans for net‑zero steel production, noting potential impacts on its own decarbonization trajectory. Its aluminium portfolio shows very low carbon intensity versus the global market, with a further 2024 decrease driven by improved client data quality, underscoring limited indirect climate impact.

- Asset management climate targets: KBC Asset Management sets targets to shift more client assets into Responsible Investing (RI), aligning with the Paris Agreement and covering unit-linked portfolios of KBC Insurance. Targets are approved by governance bodies (ISB, ExCo, Board).

- RI fund metrics and progress:
  - Increase the share of RI funds in total discretionary client money (DCM) and in total annual fund production; both are monitored monthly and are on track.
  - Reduce carbon intensity (Scope 1 and 2) of corporate investees in RI funds; coverage includes corporate bonds and equities with at least 90% GHG data availability (Trucost), excluding funds-of-funds to avoid double counting.
  - 2019 baseline deemed representative; Scope 3 excluded to improve comparability. The aggregate RI funds’ carbon intensity is already below the 2030 target, largely due to stricter fossil fuel exclusions introduced in the 2021 Investment Policy.
  - The carbon intensity reduction target is inspired by the Net Zero Asset Managers Initiative and is not based on conclusive scientific evidence.
  - No changes to targets or methodologies in FY2024.

- Own investments of KBC Insurance: A separate target to lower the carbon intensity (Scope 1 and 2) of listed equity and corporate bond holdings, using Trucost data. Performance remains firmly on track and already below the 2030 target, also driven by the 2021 Investment Policy updates. No FY2024 changes to targets or methodology.

- Emissions accounting approach: KBC calculates GHG emissions per the GHG Protocol. Over 99% of reported Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions stem from portfolio emissions (Scope 3, Category 15: Investments). For non-Category 15 Scope 3, reporting is limited to operationally controllable sources used for staff awareness (business travel, commuting, paper and water use, waste).

nodes.title: Own investments of KBC Insurance
nodes.heading: Own investments of KBC Insurance (2.2.3.1.4)
nodes.start_phrase:
Similar to our asset management activities in the previous paragraph, we have a target for the carbon intensity of the own 
investments of KBC Insurance (excluding unit-linked investments).
nodes.summary:
- Describes KBC Group’s climate targets and progress for investment portfolios, noting that the carbon intensity of Responsible Investing (RI) funds is already below the 2030 target, largely due to the rapid rollout of a strengthened 2021 Investment Policy with additional fossil-fuel exclusions.
- Details KBC Insurance’s own-investment target (listed equities and corporate bonds, excluding unit-linked): 2019 baseline 112 tCO2e per million USD revenue; 2024 value 27 (about −75% vs 2019, as of end Q3 2024); targets of −25% by 2025 (84) and −40% by 2030 (67). Progress is on track and already better than the 2030 goal.
- Explains methodology: targets cover Scope 1 and 2 emissions of corporate investments where Trucost data is available; baseline considered representative despite Scope 1–2 limitation; the carbon intensity metric is not based on conclusive scientific evidence; no changes in targets, metrics, or measurement methodology in FY2024.
- Outlines GHG accounting per the GHG Protocol: the dominant emissions source (>99% of reported Scope 1–3) is Scope 3 Category 15 (“Investments”) from lending, investment, and insurance underwriting. For other Scope 3 categories, KBC reports only operationally controllable sources (business travel, commuting, paper, water, waste) to drive staff awareness.
- Notes that management aggregates fund targets under a neutral asset allocation assumption; actual outcomes depend on asset allocation and the GHG reductions achieved by individual funds.

nodes.title: GHG emissions: gross Scope 1, 2, 3 and total emissions
nodes.heading: GHG emissions: gross Scope 1, 2, 3 and total emissions (2.2.3.2)
nodes.start_phrase:
We calculate our direct and indirect carbon footprint in accordance with the GHG Protocol Corporate Accounting and 
Reporting Standard.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on KBC Group’s climate strategy for investments and operations, highlighting targets, methodologies, results, and scope definitions for greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in 2024.
- Asset management and Responsible Investing (RI) funds: current portfolio carbon intensity is already below the 2030 target, largely due to the rapid implementation of KBC’s updated 2021 Investment Policy, which tightened fossil-fuel exclusions.
- KBC Insurance own investments:
  - Target set for carbon intensity (Scope 1 + 2) of the listed equity and corporate bond portfolio (metric: tCO2e per million USD revenue; base year 2019).
  - Progress is firmly on track and already below the 2030 target, again driven by the 2021 Investment Policy changes.
  - Scope covers corporate bonds and equities with Trucost data; baseline deemed representative, while acknowledging limitations of carbon intensity as a scientific metric.
- Group GHG accounting approach:
  - Emissions calculated per the GHG Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard.
  - Biggest source is Scope 3 Category 15 (Investments) from lending, investments, and insurance underwriting, representing over 99% of total reported Scope 1–3 emissions.
  - Non-Category 15 Scope 3 sources reported to raise staff awareness (business travel, commuting, paper, water, waste).
- 2024 scope extension: own operational carbon footprint broadened beyond financial consolidation to include entities under KBC’s operational control, with separate disclosure for consolidated vs. other controlled entities in Scope 1 and 2.
- Reported emissions snapshot (as at 30 September used as proxy for year-end):
  - Scope 1: 40,717 tCO2e.
  - Scope 2: 35,361 tCO2e (location-based) and 4,626 tCO2e (market-based).
  - Scope 3 total: 45,825,058 tCO2e, of which Category 15 (Investments) totals 45,801,394 tCO2e; White Paper sectors 26,822,564 tCO2e; remaining sectors 18,978,830 tCO2e.
  - Total GHG (market-based): 45,870,401 tCO2e.
- Investment portfolio metrics and coverage:
  - Absolute GHG for some investment portfolios not available at reporting date; carbon intensities are reported instead, covering over 97% of corporate and sovereign investments.
  - Emission intensities disclosed for asset management portfolios (corporates and sovereigns), KBC Bank’s sovereign bond portfolio, and KBC Insurance’s own investments; KBC Insurance’s corporate intensity (base 2019) shows strong reduction and is already below 2030 target.
- Methodologies and data quality:
  - Financed emissions calculated using the PCAF Global Standard (Part A for lending and leasing; Part C for insurance-associated emissions), with detailed data quality scores by sector and product line.
  - Notes on limitations: double counting in vehicle financing across certain sectors; ~5% of the loan book lacks PCAF calculations; Trucost models the latest sovereign GHG data due to a one-year reporting lag.
- Insurance-associated emissions: calculated for the Belgian portfolio per PCAF Part C with disclosed data quality scores (personal motor vs. commercial lines).
- Own operations footprint methodology:
  - >98% primary activity data; hybrid approach for Scope 1 & 2 using supplier-specific and recognized standard factors (IEA, Reliable Disclosure, AIB, UK DESNZ, and KBC-specific fallback).
  - Scope 3 Categories 1, 5, 6, 7 calculated by average-data method for awareness and internal management.
  - 2024 methodological refinements: switch to net calorific value factors for fuel; water supply moved from Category 5 to Category 1; improved extrapolation for small subsidiaries using FTE for transport and floor area for buildings (extrapolated emissions ~1.5% of total).
- Clarifications:
  - The scope of emissions reported in the comprehensive table differs from the scopes used for certain reduction targets; therefore, target columns are not filled except where aligned.
  - Emissions for non-financial assets are generally not calculated beyond those included in own operations.

nodes.title: Own carbon footprint
nodes.heading: Own carbon footprint (2.2.3.2.1)
nodes.start_phrase:
The calculation of the GHG emissions linked to our operational perimeter follows the GHG Protocol Corporate Accounting and 
Reporting Standard.
nodes.summary:
- The excerpt reports greenhouse gas (GHG) emission intensities across KBC’s investing and insurance activities, including:
  - Asset management: intensity metrics for investments in corporates (tCO2e per million USD revenue) and sovereigns (tCO2e per million USD GDP), with example values such as 58 for corporates and 532 for sovereigns.
  - KBC Bank’s sovereign bond portfolio: weighted sovereign GHG intensity (e.g., 623 tCO2e/million USD GDP), noting sovereign data is partly modelled by Trucost (S&P) due to reporting lags and updated for imported emissions (Nov 2024).
  - KBC Insurance’s own investments: emission intensities for corporates (showing a declining trend over time) and sovereigns.
  - Scope caution: except for KBC Insurance’s own corporate investments, tabled GHG scopes differ from the scopes of KBC’s reduction targets, so target columns are not filled.

- Financed emissions totals and methodology:
  - 2024 financed emissions are disclosed for several portfolios, with totals split by Scopes 1, 2, and 3 (figures provided per footnote), calculated largely under the PCAF Global Standard Part A; some portfolios have an overall data quality score of 5.0.
  - Vehicle financing emissions include operational leasing and may be double-counted where sector-specific calculations also apply; about 4.6–5% of the loan book lacks PCAF-calculable data.
  - Detailed PCAF data quality scores are listed by sector (e.g., Real Estate mortgages 3.0; operational lease 1.0; several heavy industry sectors at 5.0).
  - Insurance-associated emissions are calculated with PCAF Part C for the Belgian portfolio; data quality scores: Personal Motor Lines 2.9, commercial lines 5.

- Own operational footprint methodology and 2024 updates:
  - Calculated under the GHG Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard, covering 100% of emissions from activities under operational control; >98% based on primary data.
  - Scope 1 and 2 use a hybrid approach with supplier-specific and standard emission factors (IEA, Reliable Disclosure, AIB, UK DESNZ, KBC-specific).
  - Scope 3 operational emissions (Categories 1, 5, 6, 7) use the average-data method; categories are not material but monitored for awareness.
  - 2024 methodology changes: switch to net (vs gross) calorific values; water supply moved to Scope 3 Category 1 (treatment remains in Category 5); revised extrapolation for small subsidiaries (<100 FTE) using FTE for transport and floor area for buildings; extrapolated emissions ≈1.5% of total.

- Operational intensity metrics and energy procurement:
  - 2024 GHG intensity per FTE: 1.76 tCO2e/FTE (all activities) and 1.46 tCO2e/FTE (financial activities only), based on Scope 1, market-based Scope 2, and Scope 3 own emissions; not externally validated beyond assurance provider.
  - 87.7% of purchased energy under Scope 2 is covered by contractual instruments: 2.2% energy attribute certificates (EACs), 85.6% EACs or contracts, 0% supplier emission rates.

- Financed emissions coverage and sector focus:
  - Financed emissions are measured for loan portfolios where methods/data exist; calculations are based on 30 September 2024 portfolio figures, aligned with year-end.
  - KBC distinguishes target sectors (with reduction targets) from non-target sectors and uses these measurements to track target progress and meet regulatory expectations.
  - The Sustainable Finance Programme identified carbon-intensive sectors and key product lines via sector “White Papers”: energy, commercial real estate, agriculture, food production, building and construction, chemicals, transport, metals; and product lines mortgages, car loans, car leasing, assessing environmental impacts, dependencies, risks, and opportunities.

nodes.title: Financed emissions
nodes.heading: Financed emissions (2.2.3.2.2)
nodes.start_phrase: This section describes the calculation methodologies for our Scope 3 Category 15 financed emissions.
nodes.summary:
- Own operations metrics
  - Reports GHG intensity per FTE for 2024: 1.76 tCO2e/FTE for all activities; 1.46 tCO2e/FTE for financial activities only.
  - Scope 2 energy procurement: 87.7% covered by contractual instruments (2.2% energy attribute certificates, 85.6% energy attribute certificates or contracts, 0% supplier emission rates). Applies to all purchased electricity, heating, steam, and cooling.
  - Metrics are based on Scope 1, market-based Scope 2, and Scope 3 own emissions; not externally validated beyond the assurance provider.

- Financed emissions (Scope 3, Category 15) for lending
  - Portfolio coverage and data: calculations based on loan book as of 30 Sep 2024; 4.6% of loans lack calculable financed emissions; 2.6% of emissions calculated using primary client data.
  - Target vs non-target sectors: detailed, asset-level methods for identified high-impact target sectors and product lines; high-level sector/country factor approach for non-target sectors.
  - Methodologies and tools:
    - PCAF is the primary framework; uses latest emission factors (Mar 2024), with exceptions for real estate (Mar 2021) and energy (Mar 2022); applies PCAF inflation adjustment.
    - Portfolio impact metrics use outstanding exposure; for some targets (vehicles; cement, steel, aluminium) portfolio-weighted or granted-exposure methods are used to improve management relevance.
    - Residential real estate uses portfolio-level approximations (e.g., EPC factors, expert-based m2 values) due to limited asset-level data, with plans to upgrade data infrastructure to fully align with PCAF.
    - PACTA used for cement and steel (forward-looking, technology and intensity profiling based on ALD; client-specific data preferred when available).
    - Aluminium relies mainly on client-reported intensity; PCAF factors used where missing.
    - Non-target sectors apply aggregated exposure with country-specific PCAF activity-based factors.
  - Data, systems, and quality:
    - Dedicated data platform supports ESG and financial/risk reporting with embedded data quality controls; real estate reporting temporarily outside the platform; platform alignment to PCAF planned for 2025 reporting.
    - Publishes PCAF data quality scores; acknowledges limitations from data availability and factor updates; potential overestimation in parts scored with PCAF quality 5.
    - Recalculation policy in place; active engagement with clients/data providers when sources diverge.
  - Loan portfolio carbon intensity metrics are not assured beyond the assurance provider.

- Asset management and investments
  - Scope and data: covers DCM, KBC Insurance Group Assets, KBC Pension Fund, and unit-linked assets managed by KBC Asset Management; data sourced from Trucost (about 12% primary corporate data).
  - Corporates: weighted-average GHG intensity (Scope 1 and 2 only).
  - Sovereigns: intensity computed as territorial plus imported emissions divided by constant-USD GDP.
  - Findings: government bond portfolios (both in asset management and KBC Bank’s own sovereign portfolio) show higher GHG intensity than the EMU benchmark, driven by exposures to emerging markets and higher-intensity core countries (e.g., Belgium, Netherlands, Hungary, Czech Republic).
  - KBC Insurance own investments: methodology mirrors asset management; higher sovereign intensity than EMU benchmark due to concentration in Belgian and Czech bonds.
  - Carbon intensity metrics are not assured beyond the assurance provider; outcomes depend heavily on Trucost data quality.

- Insurance-associated emissions
  - Scope and standards: calculated per PCAF Standard Part C for personal motor lines and commercial lines; currently limited to the Belgium business unit (16.8% of insured vehicles; 51.1% of GWP in commercial lines).
  - Coverage: clients’ Scope 1 and 2; 30% of emissions based on primary data (PCAF quality levels 1–2).
  - 2024 results (Belgium): personal motor lines 99,386 tCO2e; commercial lines 100,333 tCO2e.
  - Methods:
    - Personal motor lines: uses PCAF attribution factor for Belgium; internal data on engine type, WLTP, and mileage when available; Scope 1 covers fuel combustion, Scope 2 covers electricity for EVs; third-party estimates as fallback.
    - Commercial lines: applies PCAF insurance economic emission factor database using NACE codes (tCO2e per million EUR turnover); weighted averages used where sector mapping is missing.
  - Limitations: reliance on proxies/averages where exact data is missing; lack of client-reported GHG and revenue data in commercial lines; plans to enhance data gathering and align with evolving PCAF guidance.

nodes.title: Insurance-associated emissions
nodes.heading: Insurance-associated emissions (2.2.3.2.3)
nodes.start_phrase: In 2023, we calculated the emissions of part of our insurance portfolio for the first time.
nodes.summary:
- KBC Group reports its first calculation (for 2023) of insurance-associated GHG emissions using PCAF Standard Part C, limited to personal motor lines and commercial lines, and currently disclosed only for the Belgium business unit (16.8% of group insured vehicles; 51.1% of group commercial-lines GWP).
- Scope and methodology:
  - Personal motor lines include passenger cars, motorcycles, LCVs, and motorhomes; emissions estimated via PCAF attribution factors for Belgium using vehicle engine type, WLTP values, and mileage where available; Scope 1 covers fuel combustion, Scope 2 covers electricity for EVs; third-party estimates used when internal data is missing.
  - Commercial lines emissions estimated using PCAF’s insurance-specific economic emission factor database and NACE codes (tCO2e per million euros turnover). 
  - Standard emission factors widely applied; 30% of emissions are based on primary data (PCAF data quality levels 1–2).
- Reported insurance-associated emissions (Belgium):
  - Personal motor lines: 99,386 tCO2e
  - Commercial lines: 100,333 tCO2e
- Limitations: data quality and gaps necessitating proxies/averages for vehicle data, lack of client GHG data for commercial lines, reliance on activity-based factors and weighted averages where sector mapping is missing. KBC plans to improve data collection and align with future PCAF expansions to additional insurance lines. Emissions figures are not assured by an external party beyond the assurance provider.
- GHG intensity approach: multiple intensity metrics tailored to activities—own operations per FTE; lending targets relative to sector physical outputs or financed amounts; investment portfolio targets relative to corporate revenues and sovereign GDP. No single group-wide GHG intensity metric is disclosed.
- Carbon credits and neutrality:
  - KBC offsets residual own operational emissions annually via carbon credits cancelled at the start of the following year (credits cancelled in a reporting year offset the prior year’s footprint).
  - 2024: financed 56,000 tCO2e in emission reductions/removals (90% reductions, 10% removals; all removals biogenic; 0% technological); 100% under Verra; 0% from EU projects; 56,000 credits verified and cancelled; 54,000 credits planned for cancellation in 2025 (not yet contractually secured).
  - Since 2021, own operations are net climate neutral through measure–reduce–offset; avoided emissions are not counted; projects are high-quality with co-benefits, selected via due diligence but reliant on third-party information; offsetting not validated externally beyond the assurance provider.

nodes.title: GHG intensity
nodes.heading: GHG intensity (2.2.3.2.4)
nodes.start_phrase: We have set a range of targets in terms of carbon intensity for our lending and investing activities.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines KBC Group’s approach to GHG intensity metrics across activities, with context-specific measures rather than a single total intensity metric.
- Own operations’ carbon intensity measured per FTE; lending targets tied to sector physical outputs or financed amounts; investment portfolio intensity linked to corporate revenues and sovereign GDP.
- Explains carbon offsetting process: remaining own operational emissions are offset annually via carbon credits; credits cancelled at the start of the following year relate to the prior year’s footprint, and planned 2025 cancellations are not yet contractually secured.
- Reports 2024 financed emission outcomes: 56,000 tCO2e reductions/removals (90% reductions, 10% removals), all removals biogenic; 100% under Verra Carbon Standard; no EU-issued projects; no Article 6 corresponding adjustment indicated; 56,000 credits cancelled in 2024; 54,000 planned for 2025.
- Confirms ongoing goal (since 2021) of net climate neutrality for own operations through measure–reduce–offset, with avoided emissions excluded from target achievement.
- Describes selection of high-quality, certified offset projects with co-benefits for communities and biodiversity, supported by due diligence yet dependent on third-party information and credit availability.
- Notes that offsetting is not externally validated beyond the assurance provider.

nodes.title: GHG removals and GHG mitigation projects financed through carbon credits
nodes.heading: GHG removals and GHG mitigation projects financed through carbon credits (2.2.3.3)
nodes.start_phrase: The portion of our own footprint that cannot yet be eliminated is offset using carbon credits.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines KBC Group’s approach to GHG intensity: tailored metrics by context rather than a single group-wide metric. Own operations measured per FTE; sectoral lending targets tied to sector output or financed amounts; investment portfolio intensity tied to corporate revenue and sovereign GDP.
- Describes carbon credit use for residual operational emissions: emissions are measured annually, credits contracted on calculated volumes, and cancelled at the start of the following year. Notes that planned 2025 cancellations are not yet contract-based.
- Reports 2024 climate credit figures: 56,000 tCO2e reductions/removals financed and cancelled; 90% reductions, 10% removals; all removals biogenic; 0% technological; 100% under Verra; 0% from EU projects; no Article 6 corresponding adjustments indicated; 54,000 credits planned for 2025.
- Confirms net climate neutrality for own operations since 2021 via a measure–reduce–offset strategy; avoided emissions are not counted toward reduction targets. Project selection emphasizes high-quality, certified credits with community and biodiversity co-benefits; relies on third-party information; offsetting verified only by the assurance provider.
- Details Internal Carbon Pricing (ICP) framework established in 2021, aligned with CDP/Ecofys guidance and NGFS scenarios. Prices (2024): 35 EUR/tCO2 (well-below 2°C path) and 99 EUR/tCO2 (net zero 2050 path), with expected increases by 2030 of 77% and 201% respectively.
- ICP currently applied as a shadow price in credit decisions for carbon-intensive sectors, affecting Scope 3 Category 15; about 0.5% of financed Scope 1 and 2 emissions potentially subject to ICP; none of KBC’s own Scope 1 and 2 are priced. Broader application planned as data improves (e.g., via CSRD). ICP measurement assured only within the Sustainability Statement assurance.
- Introduces Water and Marine Resources management, emphasizing policy-based oversight within the Sustainability Policy Framework.
- Biodiversity Policy: prohibits financing/insuring/advising on destructive fishing practices (including shark finning and commercial whaling) and encourages adoption of MSC/ASC standards.
- Mining Policy: acknowledges water and broader environmental/social risks; imposes strict conditions (e.g., alignment with EITI) on financing, insurance, and advisory for mining; global scope with monitoring aligned to climate-policy governance.

nodes.title: Internal carbon pricing (ICP)
nodes.heading: Internal carbon pricing (ICP) (2.2.3.4)
nodes.start_phrase:
In 2021 we established a first ICP framework which is built around the four-dimensional framework of the 2017 ‘How-to Guide to 
Corporate ICP’ report of CDP/Ecofys.
nodes.summary:
- Internal carbon pricing (ICP): KBC established an ICP framework in 2021 based on CDP/Ecofys’s four-dimensional approach, with annual reviews by Sustainability and Economic departments. ICP trajectories extend to 2050 for two NGFS-based EU transition pathways: well-below 2°C (WB2D) and net zero by 2050 (NZ2050). NGFS carbon price data are averaged across models, interpolated, adjusted to 2020 euros, and used as a uniform internal metric. For 2024, internal carbon prices are 35 EUR/t CO2 (WB2D) and 99 EUR/t CO2 (NZ2050), with assumed increases by 2030 of 77% and 201% respectively. ICP is applied as a shadow price in credit decisions for carbon-intensive sectors, currently limited to Scope 3 Category 15 (financed) emissions; about 0.5% of financed Scope 1 and 2 emissions may be influenced, while KBC’s own Scope 1 and 2 are not priced. Scope expansion is planned as data improves (e.g., via CSRD). Measurement is not externally validated beyond the Sustainability Statement assurance provider.

- Water and marine resources policies: Within the Group Sustainability Policy Framework, several policies address water-related impacts. The Biodiversity Policy prohibits financing, insurance, or advisory services tied to destructive fishing practices, shark finning, and commercial whaling, and promotes adoption of MSC and ASC standards. The Mining Policy acknowledges risks to water use and quality and other social-environmental impacts; it imposes strict conditions, including adherence to external standards such as the EITI, and applies globally across financing, insurance, and advisory services. Compliance monitoring follows the process used for climate-related policies.

structure.title: Policies related to water and marine resources
structure.heading: Policies related to water and marine resources (2.3.1.1)
structure.start_phrase:
As explained in section 2.2.2.1 on climate-related policies, our Group Sustainability Policy Framework contains different policies 
which are indirectly related to water, such as the Biodiversity Policy, Mining Policy and Energy policy.
structure.summary:
- Internal carbon pricing (ICP) framework established in 2021, aligned with CDP/Ecofys 2017 guidance, reviewed annually by Sustainability and Economic departments.
- ICP trajectories mapped to NGFS scenarios for two EU-relevant transition pathways: well-below 2°C (WB2D) and net zero 2050 (NZ2050), with model-averaged, interpolated, 2020-euro–converted carbon prices.
- Latest internal carbon prices (2024): 35 EUR/t CO2 (WB2D) and 99 EUR/t CO2 (NZ2050); assumed increases by 2030 of 77% (WB2D) and 201% (NZ2050), mirroring NGFS averages.
- ICP used as a shadow price in credit decision-making for carbon-intensive sectors; currently applied only to Scope 3 Category 15 (financed emissions).
- About 0.5% of financed Scope 1 and 2 emissions potentially subject to ICP; none of KBC’s own Scope 1 and 2 emissions priced; scope expected to expand as data improves (e.g., via CSRD).
- Carbon price measurement not externally validated beyond the Sustainability Statement assurance provider.

- Water and marine resources policy landscape embedded within KBC’s Group Sustainability Policy Framework, with indirect water links via Biodiversity, Mining, and Energy policies.
- Biodiversity Policy restricts financing/insurance/advice for destructive fishing practices (e.g., habitat-damaging methods, shark finning, commercial whaling) and encourages adoption of MSC/ASC standards.
- Mining Policy imposes strict conditions (e.g., alignment with EITI and other external standards), global scope, and established compliance monitoring.
- Operational context: KBC has sites in high-water-stress regions (e.g., parts of Flanders); potable water use is efficiently managed and closely monitored; no separate water supply policy as own water use is not a material matter.
- Water risk management integrated into enterprise risk processes: assessed in ERIM, sectoral Environmental & Social Heatmap, and NAPP standard; stepwise approach guided by improving data/methodologies.
- White Papers expanded in 2023 to cover water where material (agriculture; food & beverages) and a dedicated water White Paper planned for 2025; aim to understand impacts, risks, opportunities, and steer lending/insurance actions on water consumption, withdrawals, and discharges.
- No specific water-related targets or ambition indicators yet; effectiveness tracked via due diligence on policy compliance across lending, insurance, and advisory, supported by third-party ESG data and expert sustainability advice (including reputational risk); advice requests are monitored and disclosed; follow-up actions from White Papers are proposed to and approved by the ISB.

structure.title: Actions and resources related to water and marine resources
structure.heading: Actions and resources related to water and marine resources (2.3.1.2)
structure.start_phrase:
For more information on how water-related risk is embedded in our Risk Management Framework, we refer to section 2.2.2.2, 
which – besides climate-related actions – also sets out more general actions.
structure.summary:
- Context: KBC operates in high-water-stress areas (e.g., much of Flanders) and focuses on efficient, carefully monitored potable water use. No standalone water supply policy exists, as own water use is deemed non-material in KBC’s materiality assessment.
- Risk management: Water-related risks are integrated into KBC’s Risk Management Framework, explicitly assessed in ERIM, reflected in the sectoral Environmental & Social Heatmap for loan origination/monitoring, and covered by the NAPP standard. The approach is iterative and data-driven.
- White Papers: Scope expanded in 2023 beyond climate to include water where material (e.g., agriculture; food and beverages). A thematic White Paper on water is planned for 2025. Objectives include deepening insight into water impacts, risks, and opportunities and identifying actions to reduce negative and enhance positive impacts from lending and insurance on water use, withdrawals, and discharges.
- Metrics and targets: No specific water or marine resources targets or ambition indicators currently. Effectiveness is tracked via strict due diligence for lending, insurance, and advisory services against the sustainability framework, using third-party ESG data (including controversies).
- Governance and processes: Sustainability expert advice on water-related matters is available (and mandatory in certain domains) with reputational risk considered; the number of advice requests is monitored and reported annually. White Paper topics and follow-up actions, when feasible, are proposed and submitted to the ISB for approval.

structure.title: Targets related to water and marine resources
structure.heading: Targets related to water and marine resources (2.3.2.1)
structure.start_phrase:
At this point in time, we do not have water and marine resources-related targets in place nor have we defined any ambition level 
indicators to evaluate progress.
structure.summary:
- KBC operates in high-water-stress regions and focuses on efficient potable water use and continuous monitoring, but has no standalone water supply policy as own water use is not deemed material.
- Water-related risks are embedded in KBC’s Risk Management Framework via ERIM, a sectoral Environmental & Social Heatmap used in lending and monitoring, and the NAPP standard; the approach evolves with data and methodology improvements.
- The scope of White Papers was expanded beyond climate to include water for sectors where it is material (e.g., agriculture, food and beverages), with a dedicated water White Paper planned for 2025 to inform actions that reduce negative and enhance positive water impacts from lending and relevant insurance activities.
- KBC currently has no specific targets or ambition indicators for water and marine resources; effectiveness is tracked through strict due diligence across lending, insurance, and advisory, use of third-party ESG data (including controversies), and expert sustainability advice, which is monitored and disclosed in the Sustainability Report; White Paper follow-ups are submitted to the ISB.
- Biodiversity and ecosystems risks and dependencies are assessed through ERIM across banking, insurance, and asset management, with core-country breakdowns and short-, medium-, and long-term horizons; assessments cover both transition and physical risks across the full value chain and consider macroeconomic and systemic risk scenarios, supported by ENCORE and internal analyses.
- Findings indicate potential risks mainly materialize through downstream activities (lending, insuring, investing), especially under macroeconomic and systemic conditions, and are integrated into core risk processes (Risk Appetite, ICAAP/ILAAP/ORSA) reported to executive and board bodies.
- KBC’s Sustainability Policy Framework includes policies directly or indirectly tied to biodiversity (Biodiversity Policy, Mining Policy, Exclusion Policy for responsible investing) and client requirements on sustainable land use, agriculture, oceans, and deforestation.
- Biodiversity-related opportunities are not considered material and are therefore not covered.

structure.title: Transition plan and consideration of biodiversity and ecosystems in strategy and business model
structure.heading: Transition plan and consideration of biodiversity and ecosystems in strategy and business model (2.4.1.1)
structure.start_phrase:
We acknowledge that our impacts and dependencies on biodiversity and ecosystems can influence our strategy and business 
model, and can thus result in risks and opportunities.
structure.summary:
- KBC recognizes that its impacts and dependencies on biodiversity and ecosystems can affect its strategy and business model, creating risks and opportunities.
- Biodiversity-related risks are analyzed through KBC’s ERIM, assessing materiality across the group and separately for banking, insurance, and asset management, with further breakdowns for core countries.
- Risks are evaluated over short (0–3 years), medium (3–10 years), and long-term (beyond 10 years) horizons.
- Expert assessments cover impacts across all traditional risk types and the full value chain.
- Both transition and physical risks are considered: physical risk assessment is used to identify dependencies; transition risk assessment is used to identify impacts on nature.
- Analyses incorporate potential future macroeconomic developments and systemic risks, supported by tools such as ENCORE and other internal exercises.
- Potential risks are expected to materialize mainly through downstream activities (lending, insuring, investing), especially under macroeconomic and systemic risk scenarios.
- Findings feed into core risk management processes (Risk Appetite, ICAAP/ILAAP/ORSA) and are reported regularly to the ExCo, RCC, and Board.
- KBC has a Sustainability Policy Framework addressing biodiversity and ecosystems, including a Biodiversity Policy, Mining Policy, and an Exclusion Policy for responsible investment funds.
- The framework sets requirements for clients on sustainable land use, sustainable agriculture practices, sustainable oceans, and includes measures to address deforestation.
- Biodiversity-related opportunities are deemed non-material per KBC’s materiality assessment and are not covered in this document.

structure.title: Policies related to biodiversity and ecosystems
structure.heading: Policies related to biodiversity and ecosystems (2.4.2.1)
structure.start_phrase: We have policies in place to manage our material impacts and risks related to biodiversity and ecosystems.
structure.summary:
- Scope and context: KBC Group’s 2024 Annual Report section on Biodiversity and Ecosystems (2.4) outlines how nature-related impacts, dependencies, risks and opportunities influence strategy, risk management and policies across banking, insurance and asset management.

- Strategy and risk assessment (2.4.1):
  - Biodiversity loss and ecosystem damage are assessed through the Enterprise-wide Risk Identification Methodology (ERIM), with separate views for banking, insurance, and asset management and further breakdowns by core countries.
  - Time horizons: short (0–3 years), medium (3–10 years), long (10+ years).
  - Both transition and physical risks considered; dependencies assessed via physical risk analysis; impacts assessed via transition risk analysis.
  - Inputs include ENCORE and internal analyses.
  - Key finding: risks are most likely to materialize through downstream activities (lending, insuring, investing), especially via macroeconomic and systemic effects.
  - Integration into core risk processes: Risk Appetite, ICAAP/ILAAP/ORSA, reported to ExCo, RCC and Board.

- Policies and governance (2.4.2.1):
  - Sustainability Policy Framework includes:
    - Biodiversity Policy: requirements for producers/traders of forest commodities; restrictions for activities in/near protected areas; rules on endangered/invasive species; provisions for cattle and fisheries; exclusions for certain unconventional oil & gas; restrictions in forestry and fisheries; animal welfare exclusions; supports traceability via recognized certifications; addresses value-chain impacts and social safeguards.
    - Mining Policy: restrictions to mitigate environmental impacts (GHG, land-use change, water/air pollution) and human rights risks; sets risk standards for lending and investments.
    - Exclusion Policy for Responsible Investing (RI) funds: excludes issuers with high/severe land-use/biodiversity controversies; excludes non-certified operators in fishing, palm oil, soy, beef, cocoa, sugarcane; addresses animal welfare (fur/special leather); applies controversy screening and certification requirements; embeds consideration of physical and transition risks in all RI funds; supports value-chain traceability.
  - Biodiversity-related opportunities deemed non-material per materiality assessment.

- Actions and resources (2.4.2.2):
  - Progressive integration of biodiversity risks into the Risk Management Framework aligned with data/methodology advances.
  - Completed actions:
    - Assessed biodiversity transition and physical risks in ERIM; embedded in sectoral Environmental & Social Heatmap for origination and monitoring.
    - Published White Papers expanding beyond climate to biodiversity; 2024 paper focused on deforestation and related risks/opportunities in lending.
    - High-level assessment of portfolio biodiversity impacts and dependencies.
    - Incorporated biodiversity-related scenarios into internal stress testing (e.g., infectious disease impacts on life insurance).
    - Included biodiversity risks within the NAPP standard.
    - Strengthened RI exclusions and screening for specific farming sectors (fishing, palm oil, soy, beef, cocoa, sugarcane).
  - Not used: biodiversity offsets, local/indigenous knowledge, or nature-based solutions in actions.

- Metrics and targets (2.4.3.1):
  - No biodiversity-related targets, ambitions, or KPIs defined yet.
  - Effectiveness monitored via strict due diligence processes (aligned with approach used for water/marine resources).

- Overall emphasis:
  - Clear risk-based approach prioritizing policy controls, sectoral exclusions, certification-driven traceability and safeguards, and integration into enterprise risk processes, with current focus on managing risks rather than setting quantitative biodiversity targets.

structure.title: Actions and resources related to biodiversity and ecosystems
structure.heading: Actions and resources related to biodiversity and ecosystems (2.4.2.2)
structure.start_phrase: For an overview of the continuous efforts that we make to integrate biodiversity risks into our Risk Management Framework and processes, we refer to section 2.2.2.2.
structure.summary:
- KBC is progressively integrating biodiversity risks into its Risk Management Framework, aligning follow-up actions with improving data and methodologies.
- Key actions: assessed biodiversity transition and physical risks in ERIM; integrated results into the sectoral Environmental & Social Heatmap; produced a White Paper on biodiversity loss focused on deforestation; executed a high-level assessment of biodiversity impacts and dependencies in the loan portfolio; incorporated biodiversity-related scenarios into internal stress tests (e.g., infectious disease impacts on life insurance); brought biodiversity risks under the NAPP standard.
- Expanded the White Paper program beyond climate to biodiversity topics in agriculture, food and beverages, and construction; 2024 featured a dedicated deforestation paper assessing lending-related risks and opportunities.
- Strengthened the Exclusion Policy for Responsible Investing funds with biodiversity screens for fishing, palm oil, soybean and beef cattle farming, and cocoa and sugarcane farming (farm-stage only), excluding firms that fail to meet biodiversity best practices.
- No use of biodiversity offsets; no incorporation of local/indigenous knowledge or nature-based solutions in actions.
- No biodiversity-specific targets, ambition levels, or KPIs; effectiveness is monitored via a strict due diligence process, consistent with the approach used for water and marine resources.

structure.title: Targets related to biodiversity and ecosystems
structure.heading: Targets related to biodiversity and ecosystems (2.4.3.1)
structure.start_phrase: We do not have biodiversity-related targets in place, nor have we defined a level of ambition or qualitative or quantitative indicators to evaluate progress.
structure.summary:
- Biodiversity risk management: KBC is integrating biodiversity transition and physical risks into its Risk Management Framework, including the sectoral Environmental & Social Heatmap for lending and monitoring. It has conducted a high-level assessment of biodiversity impacts and dependencies in its loan portfolio, incorporated biodiversity-related elements into internal stress tests (e.g., infectious disease impacts on life insurance), and brought biodiversity risks within scope of the NAPP standard.
- Thought leadership: KBC expanded its White Papers beyond climate to biodiversity topics in agriculture, food and beverages, and construction. In 2024 it published a dedicated White Paper on deforestation, assessing related risks and opportunities in lending.
- Responsible investing exclusions: The Exclusion Policy for Responsible Investing funds now includes additional biodiversity screening for fishing, palm oil and soybean farming, beef cattle ranching, and cocoa and sugarcane farming, excluding firms not complying with best biodiversity practices. The scope covers farming activities only, not downstream processing.
- Approach limitations: KBC did not use biodiversity offsets and did not incorporate local/indigenous knowledge or nature-based solutions in its biodiversity actions.
- Metrics and targets: KBC has no biodiversity-specific targets, ambitions, or indicators; it monitors effectiveness through strict due diligence, aligned with its approach to water and marine resource targets.
- Social information – own workforce: Policies aim to manage workforce-related impacts and mitigate operational, litigation, and reputational risks. The Employee Code of Conduct sets expectations aligned with KBC’s PEARL+ values, emphasizes responsible behavior, stakeholder balance, entrepreneurial mindset, lifelong learning, diversity, equal treatment, respect, and regulatory compliance. Policies are published on kbc.com.

structure.title: Policies related to own workforce
structure.heading: Policies related to own workforce (3.1.1.1)
structure.start_phrase: We have the following policies in place to manage our material impacts on our own workforce.
structure.summary:
- Focus area: KBC Group’s Social information on “Own workforce,” detailing policies, governance, and engagement practices to manage impacts, risks, and opportunities related to employees.
- Code of Conduct for employees: Sets expected behaviors aligned with PEARL+ values; covers respect, diversity and equal treatment, client/employee data discretion, whistleblowing, compliance, and speak-up culture. Mandatory training for all staff; Board approval; business units responsible for application; aligned with UN Global Compact and OECD Guidelines; stakeholder balance (clients, employees, shareholders, society).
- Whistleblower Protection Policy and Procedure: Broad scope (employees and, for certain financial-law breaches, all stakeholders including consumers); multiple reporting channels; strict confidentiality and anti-retaliation; independent investigations; Compliance reports to ExCo and RCC; recurring awareness and training; approved by ExCo and consulted with social partners.
- Remuneration governance:
  - Remuneration Policy for the Board and ExCo: Aligned with strategy (including sustainability), risk appetite, law/regulation; gender-neutral pay; competitive base pay reflecting responsibilities; collective responsibility emphasis for ExCo. Approved by General Meeting; Board/Remuneration Committee oversee implementation; respects Corporate Governance Code.
  - Group Remuneration Policy (all staff): Market-aligned, risk-aware, sustainability-aligned, gender-neutral equal pay; performance management with objectives, continuous feedback, self/peer input, calibration; fixed/variable mix with defined caps; special rules for Key Identified Staff (non-cash instruments, deferral, performance/risk alignment). Reporting aligned with supervisors/EBA; public “Compensation Report.”
- Diversity and Inclusion Policy: Zero tolerance for discrimination/harassment; emphasis on equal opportunities, with focus on gender diversity and disability inclusion; top-down accountability (ExCo, managers, employees); Corporate HR Culture Unit and local HR lead agenda; engagement with ERG “Diversity Rocks,” trade unions, HR, and a disability advisory group; annual reporting to ExCo and Board; publicly disclosed.
- Human Rights Policy: Commitment to ILO core conventions, UN Guiding Principles, OECD Guidelines, UN Global Compact, UK Modern Slavery Act, UDHR; references Code of Conduct and Whistleblower Policy; multiple channels for addressing impacts (Works Council, prevention advisory councils, HR mediators, whistleblower tool); ExCo holds highest responsibility; accident prevention policy in all core countries; prohibited practices (trafficking, forced/child labour) covered by law.
- Worker engagement and representation: Semi-annual employee engagement surveys with CEO/HR accountability; results inform organizational decisions; effectiveness tracked via response and satisfaction rates; ongoing social dialogue and formal representation on reward, employment conditions, reorganizations, and well-being; active Employee Resource Groups (Diversity Rocks; Proud@CSOB; Proud@KBC for LGBTQIA+).

structure.title: Processes for engaging with own workers and workers’ representatives about impacts
structure.heading: Processes for engaging with own workers and workers’ representatives about impacts (3.1.1.2)
structure.start_phrase: The perspectives and views of the own workforce inform our decisions and activities through considering the actual and potential impacts on the own workforce.
structure.summary:
- Sets out KBC Group’s 2024 Human Rights Policy and commitment to respect human rights for all stakeholders, especially its own workforce, aiming to minimize negative impacts/risks.
- Aligns with major international standards and laws: UN Guiding Principles, OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, ILO core conventions, UN Global Compact, UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, UK Modern Slavery Act, and national labour codes (which exceed these standards). Has workplace accident prevention policies in all core countries. Notes that trafficking, forced/compulsory and child labour are not explicitly addressed in internal workforce policies because they are prohibited by law.
- Governance and scope: Policy applies to clients, suppliers, and employees; the Executive Committee holds ultimate responsibility for sustainability and human rights.
- Related internal policies and compliance: References the Code of Conduct and a Whistleblower Protection Policy aligned with EU Directive 2019/1937; multiple internal channels (Workers’ Councils, prevention advisory councils, HR mediators) to address human rights impacts.
- Workforce engagement: Semiannual employee engagement surveys, ongoing social dialogue, and formal employee representation on reward, employment conditions, reorganisations, and well-being; CEO and HR managers accountable for survey execution and follow-up; effectiveness tracked via response and satisfaction rates. Employee Resource Groups promote inclusion (e.g., Diversity Rocks; Proud@CSOB and Proud@KBC for LGBTQIA+).
- Prevention, remediation, and reporting: Emphasis on top-management culture-setting and employee accountability; Code of Conduct, responsible behavior compass, awareness and mandatory training, speak-up culture, and a Diversity & Inclusion Policy prohibiting discrimination and disrespect. Robust, confidential, and retaliation-protected reporting via whistleblower tool, website, mailbox, local compliance, supervisors, HR leadership, employee representatives, Workers’ Council, prevention counsellors, and HR mediators; independent investigations of all cases.
- Risk mitigation and actions: Follows a local embeddedness approach—no groupwide key actions; countries implement context-specific initiatives. Examples include Hungary’s 2024 well-being focus groups (2025 rollout), Belgium’s Team Blue Challenge (volunteering; 2025 first aid and blood/plasma donation to enhance safety), Czech academies supporting parents and fathers, and Bulgaria’s “Healthy! Compass for a Better Life” publication. These initiatives are not considered material at group level for this statement.

structure.title: Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for own workers to raise concerns
structure.heading: Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for own workers to raise concerns (3.1.1.3)
structure.start_phrase: As a general approach, we put in place several preventive measures to avoid negative impacts on our own workforce:
structure.summary:
- Outlines KBC Group’s preventive approach to avoid negative impacts on its workforce, with top management responsible for culture and all employees accountable for responsible behavior.
- Highlights supporting policies and actions: Code of Conduct and trainings, promotion of a speak-up culture, and a Diversity & Inclusion Policy with zero tolerance for discrimination and disrespect.
- Details a whistleblower process enabling reports via intranet tool, website, dedicated mailbox, and face-to-face with local compliance; ensures independent, confidential, impartial investigations, confidentiality of identity, and protection against retaliation.
- Lists alternative reporting routes: supervisors, HR leadership, employee representatives, Workers’ Council, prevention counsellor, and HR mediator (or country equivalents).
- Describes the “local embeddedness” approach: no groupwide key actions for workforce issues; each country/business defines initiatives suited to its context.

structure.title: Policies related to consumers and end-users
structure.heading: Policies related to consumers and end-users (3.2.1.1)

structure.title: Business conduct policies and corporate culture
structure.heading: Business conduct policies and corporate culture (4.1.1.1)
structure.start_phrase: Responsible business conduct is crucial for KBC.
structure.summary:
- Emphasis on responsible business conduct as the basis for stakeholder trust, backed by a strong corporate culture and extensive mandatory training and awareness (99% completion in 2024), with explicit ExCo and Board commitment and zero-tolerance statements.
- Sustainability Policy Framework positions responsible behaviour and business ethics as the foundation of KBC’s sustainability approach.
- Integrity Policy defines ethical behaviour, conduct risk and compliance risk management, covering AML/CTF and embargoes, tax fraud prevention, investor and consumer protection, complaints handling, data protection/privacy, ethics and responsible behaviour, fraud coordination, anti-discrimination, governance and outsourcing/sustainability regulation compliance; roles and accountability of the Compliance function are specified.
- Code of Conduct for employees details expectations on AML/CTF, anti-fraud, market integrity, data confidentiality, client focus and conduct risk, tax compliance, anti-corruption, conflicts of interest, gifts/entertainment/sponsorship, whistleblowing/speak-up, and competition rules.
- Anti-Corruption and Bribery Policy sets zero tolerance, governance of the anti-corruption programme, accounting controls, independent investigations, annual risk assessments, internal controls and reporting, third-party due diligence/contract clauses, and integration into investment screening; highlights high-risk functions; aligned with UN Global Compact Principle 10 and OECD Guidelines.
- Whistleblower Protection Policy provides protected (including anonymous) channels, covers EU Directive 2019/1937 areas and extends to unethical conduct affecting KBC’s credibility; investigations handled independently; protections extended to anyone reporting in financial services; results reported to ExCo.
- Group Anti-Money Laundering Policy mandates KYC/KYT, local procedures aligned with EBA guidance, and recurrent monitoring/quality controls.
- Dealing Code prevents insider dealing and market manipulation via prohibited conduct rules, reporting duties, blocking periods for key employees, FSMA notifications, and compliance oversight.
- Ethics and Fraud Policy establishes a comprehensive fraud risk management process (culture, risk assessments, prevention, detection, response, monitoring/reporting) to protect KBC’s reputation and assets and those of stakeholders.
- Tax Strategy commits to responsible taxation, no assistance in tax avoidance, independent Tax function involvement in product/process approvals, proactive risk management, and transparency (including country-by-country reporting and rulings).
- Sustainability Code of Conduct for Suppliers requires adherence to social, ethical and environmental principles; enables screening, ongoing monitoring and contract termination for unresolved violations; aligned with UN Global Compact; applies to suppliers and their groups.
- Corporate culture reinforced through the Responsible Behaviour Compass and PEARL+ values (be respectful, responsive, result-driven); biannual engagement surveys; broad speak-up culture (peer, management, whistleblowing) with sanctions for violations.
- Supplier relationship management includes timely and equitable payments (including SMEs), ESG risk controls in selection and lifecycle: blacklist for controversial activities (e.g., nuclear weapons, white phosphorus), onboarding checks (financial health, embargoes, lawsuits), ESG questionnaires for larger purchases, contractual adherence to the supplier code, and monthly monitoring via internal alerts.
- Integration of governance topics into risk management: risk appetite objectives for culture/governance/compliance; NAPP process assesses conduct, fraud, sustainability, AML, embargoes, tax fraud and regulatory compliance risks; management quality evaluated for large corporates during loan origination.

structure.summary:
- Corporate culture: KBC’s culture is built on three interlinked core values—be respectful, responsive, and result-driven—captured in the PEARL+ framework established in 2012 by the Executive Committee. Culture is measured via biannual employee engagement surveys. Responsible behavior is expected from all employees, with encouragement to speak up at peer, managerial, and whistleblowing levels; violations of the Employee Code of Conduct are sanctioned.

- Supplier relationship management: KBC commits to timely payment per contract terms, monitors performance at a management-level steering committee, and treats all suppliers, including SMEs, equally. ESG risk management spans the full supplier lifecycle: an ESG-based blacklist excludes controversial activities (e.g., nuclear weapons, white phosphorus); onboarding includes checks on financial health, embargoes, lawsuits, and convictions; an ESG questionnaire is required for purchases above EUR 250,000 (and others as appropriate); ESG transparency can be a positive selection factor. Suppliers must accept the Sustainability Code of Conduct; performance and risks are monitored continuously, with monthly screenings and periodic reviews of ESG monitoring within procurement processes.

- Business conduct and governance risk: ESG (including governance) is integrated into the Risk Management Framework and compliance. Risk appetite includes objectives for culture, governance, and risk/compliance. Governance risks are assessed via NAPP for conduct risk, fraud, sustainability, AML, embargoes, tax fraud, and regulatory non-compliance. Management quality of large corporates is assessed during loan origination.

structure.title: Actions in relation to business conduct policies
structure.heading: Actions in relation to business conduct policies (4.1.1.3)
structure.start_phrase: In addition to the above-mentioned policies, we have actions in place to manage, assess and follow up the impacts and risks related to business conduct matters.
structure.summary:
- Corporate culture and values: KBC’s culture is built on “be respectful, be responsive, be result-driven,” encapsulated in PEARL+. Culture set by the Executive Committee, monitored via biannual employee engagement surveys. Emphasis on responsible behaviour, accountability, and a strong speak‑up environment (peer, line management, whistleblowing), with sanctions for Code of Conduct violations.
- Supplier relationship management: Commitment to timely payments with management-level monitoring; equal treatment of all suppliers including SMEs. ESG risk management embedded in procurement: blacklist of suppliers involved in controversial activities (e.g., nuclear weapons, white phosphorus); onboarding screening for financial health, embargoes, lawsuits, convictions; ESG questionnaires for purchases above 250,000 euros and when appropriate; ESG information encouraged as a positive selection criterion. Mandatory adherence to the Sustainability Code of Conduct for Suppliers; ongoing performance monitoring and monthly alerts; periodic reviews of ESG monitoring within procurement processes and tools.
- Business conduct and governance integration: ESG (including governance) risks integrated into the Risk Management Framework and risk appetite, with objectives promoting culture, governance, and risk/compliance. NAPP process assesses governance-related risks (conduct risk, fraud, sustainability, AML, embargoes, tax fraud, regulatory non-compliance) and defines actions. Management quality evaluated for large corporates in loan origination.
- Compliance risk management: Focus on integrity and conduct risk; protection of consumers, investors, and policyholders; AML/CFT, anti-corruption/bribery, ethics, and corporate governance. Executive Committee and top management are accountable; compliance function provides oversight and monitoring.
- Anti-corruption and bribery framework: Policies and controls include conflict of interest rules; gifts/entertainment/donations/sponsorship policy; due diligence and pre-employment screening for boards/top management; four‑eye recruitment; accounting controls; annual entity-level risk assessments (country, sector, transaction, opportunity, partnership, due diligence risks); mandatory training; first-line preventive controls with compliance monitoring; breach record-keeping. Supported by whistleblower protection, speak-up culture, AML policy, and supplier code (with anti-corruption due diligence and contractual clauses). Independent investigations under compliance supervision; outcomes reported to local management, ExCo, Group ExCo, and RCC.

structure.title: Prevention and detection of corruption and bribery
structure.heading: Prevention and detection of corruption and bribery (4.1.1.4)
structure.start_phrase: We have established several procedures to prevent, detect and address allegations or incidents of corruption and bribery.
structure.summary:
- Focus on compliance risk management emphasizing integrity, ethical behavior, conduct risk, and core domains: consumer/investor/policyholder protection, anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing, anti-corruption and bribery, ethics and responsible behavior, and corporate governance.
- Governance: Executive Committee and top management hold primary accountability; the compliance function plays a fundamental, supporting and monitoring role.
- Anti-corruption and bribery framework: conflict of interest policies; gifts/entertainment/donations/sponsorship policy; due diligence and pre-employment screening for board and top management; four-eye principle in recruitment; specific accounting controls; annual entity-level anti-bribery risk assessments (covering country, sector, transaction, business opportunity, partnership, and due diligence risks); mandatory staff training and awareness; first-line controls with compliance monitoring; breach record-keeping.
- Supporting policies and culture: Whistleblower Protection Policy, speak-up culture (Code of Conduct), Anti-Money Laundering Policy, and Supplier Sustainability Code of Conduct with anti-corruption due diligence and contractual clauses.
- Investigations: handled by an independent investigation unit under compliance supervision; results reported to local management/ExCo, Group ExCo, and the RCC.
- Business conduct metrics and targets:
  - Confirmed incidents: no convictions or fines for anti-corruption/anti-bribery violations in the reporting period; information not externally validated beyond the assurance provider.
  - Payment practices: standard payment term of 30 days after correct invoice receipt applied to ~88% of annual invoice value across KBC and subsidiaries; 5-day term for Bulgarian leasing invoices (~11% of annual invoices); <1% of invoices have deviating terms due to local or contractual specifics.
  - 2024 performance: average of 16 days between invoice receipt and payment; calculated for the first time for the Sustainability Statement, based on actual invoice data in five core countries; excludes employee payments, intra-group items, and tax authority payments; consolidated as a weighted average by number of invoices; not externally validated beyond the assurance provider.
  - Causes of late payment mainly processing issues (e.g., incorrect invoices); blocked invoices and resolution times are reported to Procurement management.
  - No outstanding legal proceedings for late payments.

structure.title: Confirmed incidents
structure.heading: Confirmed incidents (4.1.2.1)
structure.start_phrase: KBC has no convictions nor received any fines for violating anti-corruption and anti-bribery laws during the reporting period.
structure.summary:
- Scope: KBC Group Annual Report 2024, Business conduct metrics and targets (4.1.2), covering confirmed incidents and payment practices.
- Anti-corruption/bribery: No convictions or fines during the reporting period; information assured only by the assurance provider (no separate external validation).
- Payment policy: Commitment to on-time supplier payments, including SMEs. Standard term is 30 days after receipt of a correct invoice, applied to about 88% of annual invoice value across KBC and subsidiaries. Leasing activities in Bulgaria (11% of invoices) use a 5-day term. Fewer than 1% of invoices deviate due to local or contract-specific negotiations.
- 2024 performance metric: Average payment occurred 16 days after invoice receipt. This is a first-time, assured-only metric based on actual invoice data from KBC and subsidiaries in five core countries; excludes employee payments, intra-group items, and tax authorities. The consolidated figure is a weighted average by number of invoices.
- Causes of late payments: Mostly processing issues (e.g., incorrect amounts, prices, or VAT). A dedicated team resolves these and reports blocked-invoice counts and resolution times to Procurement management.
- Legal status: No outstanding legal proceedings related to late payments.

structure.title: Payment practices
structure.heading: Payment practices (4.1.2.2)
structure.start_phrase: As mentioned in section 4.1.1.2, KBC is committed to paying all its invoices from suppliers (including suppliers which are SMEs) on time.
structure.summary:
- Focus: Business conduct metrics and targets (Annual Report KBC Group 2024, section 4.1.2), covering confirmed incidents and payment practices.
- Confirmed incidents (4.1.2.1): No convictions or fines for anti-corruption or anti-bribery during the reporting period; information not externally validated beyond the assurance provider.
- Payment practices (4.1.2.2):
  - Commitment to on-time payment for all suppliers, including SMEs.
  - Standard payment term of 30 days after receipt of a correct invoice applies to about 88% of annual invoice value across KBC and subsidiaries, equally for all suppliers and invoice types.
  - For leasing activities in Bulgaria (11% of annual invoices), standard payment term is 5 days.
  - Fewer than 1% of invoices have different terms due to local subsidiary practices or individual contract negotiations.
  - In 2024, the average time from invoice receipt to payment was 16 days; first-time calculation for the Sustainability Statement; not externally validated beyond the assurance provider.
  - Methodology: based on actual invoice data from five core countries; excludes employee payments, intra-group items, and tax authorities; consolidated as a weighted average by number of invoices.
  - Delays typically stem from processing issues (e.g., incorrect invoices with mismatched amounts, prices, or VAT); a dedicated team reports blocked invoices and resolution times to Procurement management.
  - No outstanding legal proceedings related to late payments.
